[Elsa 4 Lead] On behalf of @sfmskywalker.

🔥

# Elsa 4 multi-tenancy program

Status: **In progress, Phase 0 starting (11 Nov 2026).**
Assessment: [#4123](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/issues/4123) (read-only investigation, pinned to foundation `67c5da40d`). Sibling program: #4132 (embedding Elsa 4 in your own app). Parity program: #2771 (ADR 0085, Phase 3 "tenancy, Elsa 3 import").
Owner authorization: Sipke, 11 Nov 2026, 16:00 (Europe/Amsterdam), in chat with Elsa 4 Lead: turn the assessment into a durable program on GitHub and start it.

**Governance note.** This repo's active programs are the rows of the program-goal registry, each named by an owner amendment to [ADR 0080 D0](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/main/docs/adr/0080-elsa-4-simplification-decisions.md#d0--focus). The amendment text and the registry rows are not written yet: see #4135. Sipke's chat message is the authorization; the ADR/registry record is bookkeeping. The `ready-for-agent` cap (20) is not touched: no child is labelled `ready-for-agent`; a maintainer promotes children when they are picked.

## Goal

Elsa 4 can host many tenants safely in one process and database: a tenant is resolved per request, bound once, carried explicitly through every asynchronous boundary, and isolated in every store, with a shared two-tenant conformance suite proving it. Context: Elsa Cloud's high-density hosting on Elsa 3 (elsa-control #633); Elsa 4 should be able to host the same way later.

## Hard requirements

1. **Tenancy lives at the provider-abstraction / store-contract level, never tightly coupled to EF Core.** Correctness comes from the domain-owned store contracts and `PersistenceAccessContext` (ADR 0073 D2), not from EF-only mechanisms (global query filters, `DbContext` model tricks, interceptors). EF stores honour the contract; in-memory stores must pass the same suite.
2. **Elsa 3 is a reference only** (resolver pipeline concept, host/header/route/claim resolvers, lifecycle events, per-tenant fairness). Do not copy its ambient `AsyncLocal` plus global-filter design or its three-valued tenant visibility.
3. **Recommended model (v1): shared-table discriminator.** Database-per-tenant (shell-per-tenant) is an opt-in hybrid later (Phase 5) that reuses the Phase 1 contract unchanged. Schema-per-tenant is proposed as rejected. Both need Sipke's confirmation (Q3).
4. **Explicit scope propagation across async boundaries:** explicit and persisted at every asynchronous boundary; ambient only inside one DI scope.
5. **A two-tenant conformance suite is a gate**, not a nice-to-have: shared, run against every store (in-memory and EF, all four providers) plus an architecture guard against unscoped reads.
6. **Identity Phase 1 (#2775, #2777–#2782) is built tenant-aware from the start**, not retrofitted.

## Non-goals (v1)

- A non-EF provider SPI or a real provider layer below the stores (only if Q1 is answered "stronger").
- Per-tenant identity providers or per-tenant OpenIddict stores (ADR 0085 D6 keeps identity host-wide in v1; revisit with Q8/Q9).
- Copying Elsa 3's tenant model, or Elsa 3 tenant import (parity Phase 3 owns import; Q5).
- Quotas and billing (Q11) and any Elsa Cloud control-plane work.
- A Studio tenant switcher before Phase 3.

## Phases

Sizes from the assessment: S ≤ 1 engineer-week, M 1–3, L 3–6. **All effort figures below are unspiked estimates** (read-only assessment, no builds or tests). The Phase 0 spike exists to validate them.

| Phase | Scope | Assessment workstreams | Effort (unspiked) | Exit criteria |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **0. Decide and validate** | ADR; estimate-validating spike; program bookkeeping | W0 (+ spike) | ADR 0.5–1 wk; spike ≈ 1 wk (my proposal) | ADR agreed by its named approvers; spike report posted with a revised estimate table and the audit of the 13 unscoped stores; confirmed leaks filed as separate issues |
| **1. Foundations** | Move scope primitives to `Elsa.Persistence.Core`; tenant catalog; resolver pipeline and binder; unified contract style; pump fallbacks fail closed; two-tenant conformance suite (first run against what exists); identity Phase 1 tenant-aware addendum | W1, W2, part of W3, part of W4, W8a | ≈ 8–12 wk (my sum of shares of W1 1–2, W2 3–5, W3 part, W4 part, W8a part; not separately estimated) | Resolver binds the scope per request and fails closed on none; catalog on all four providers with migrations; conformance suite green in CI on in-memory and EF SQLite and wired for the other providers; bugs it finds filed separately; #3701 fixed or closed with evidence |
| **2. Audit and close** | Fix unscoped stores, lock keys, extension stores, HTTP routing and trigger isolation; real-host second-tenant journey | W4, W6, W8b | W4 3–5, W6 1–3, W8b share | Every store passes the suite or is documented host-wide; second-tenant journey passes on a real host (closes #3701 and the tenant half of #4107) |
| **3. Identity** | Tenant-parametrised users/roles, host vs tenant permissions, support context, tenant selection at sign-in, Studio switcher | W5, W7 | W5 4–6, W7 1–2 | Cross-tenant admin through an explicit expiring audited context; tenant A cannot list tenant B's users (per-endpoint test) |
| **4. Operations** | Per-tenant metrics, quotas/limits, export/delete, lifecycle hooks | W9 (+ rest of W3) | 1–3 (+ W3 1–3 overall) | Noisy-neighbour limits proven; tenant delete/export tested |
| **5. Optional hybrid** | Database-per-tenant via shell-per-tenant, migration orchestration over N databases, density measurements (#2757) | W10 | +5–10 | Only if a Dedicated tier needs it |

**Totals (unspiked):** discriminator v1 (W0–W9) ≈ **20–36 engineer-weeks**; hybrid **+5–10**. Assumptions: EF-only family, PostgreSQL/SQL Server primary, identity Phase 1 lands first, Studio reuses the identity admin screens.

## Ordered checklist

### Phase 0
- [ ] #4133 ADR: multi-tenancy invariant, vocabulary, resolution order, support-context model, host-wide vs tenant-keyed
- [ ] #4134 Spike: validate the multi-tenancy estimate with two real scopes
- [ ] #4135 Record the multi-tenancy and embedding programs in ADR 0080 D0 and the program-goal registry

### Phase 1
- [ ] #4136 Move scope primitives to `Elsa.Persistence.Core` (W1)
- [ ] #4137 Tenant catalog contract, in-memory store and first-party scope source (W2)
- [ ] #4138 Tenant catalog EF stores and migrations on four providers (W2)
- [ ] #4139 Tenant resolver pipeline and request binder (W2)
- [ ] #4140 Unify the store-contract style: explicit tenant ids are verified against the bound scope (W4)
- [ ] #4141 Background pumps fail closed instead of defaulting to `default` (W3)
- [ ] #4142 Two-tenant conformance suite: harness and Runtime stores (W8a)
- [ ] #4143 Two-tenant conformance suite: remaining stores and provider matrix (W8a)
- [ ] #4144 Architecture guard: fail on a store read that ignores the bound scope (W8a)
- [ ] #4145 Identity Phase 1 tenant-awareness addendum for #2775, #2777–#2782 (W5 prerequisite)

### Phase 2 (not filed yet)
- [ ] Store audit fixes: the unscoped stores that need a decision (`EfRuleRunStore`, `EfEtlConnectorSourceBudget`, `EfWorkflowExecutionDeletionStore`, `EfWorkflowLibraryStore` partials)
- [ ] Scope-prefixed lock keys (Design `workflow-draft:{id}`, `workflow-definition:{id}`; task locks)
- [ ] Extension stores and message envelopes carry the tenant (#3583 messaging, Agents, ETL, Rules, Weaver)
- [ ] Tenant-qualified HTTP route table and host/header/route resolvers (W6)
- [ ] Per-tenant due-batch limits and fairness for timers and recovery
- [ ] Real-host second-tenant journey on the Workbench (#3701, #4107 tenant half)

### Phase 3 (not filed yet)
- [ ] Tenant-parametrised identity API and Studio (after #2777–#2782), host vs tenant permissions, `*` definition
- [ ] Support context (#838 idea): target-bound, expiring, audited; host-admin permission
- [ ] Tenant selection at sign-in or token exchange; OpenIddict decision
- [ ] Studio tenant switcher and tenant-aware backends and preferences

### Phase 4 (not filed yet)
- [ ] Per-tenant metrics, quotas and limits; tenant export and delete; lifecycle hooks for pumps

### Phase 5 (optional, not filed yet)
- [ ] Per-scope connection resolver, per-tenant database provisioning, migration orchestrator over N databases, shell-per-tenant composition, density measurements (#2757)

## Existing issues reused (linked, not refiled)

#3701 (packaged Workflows Design stores every definition under the default tenant: root cause is the missing resolver/binder, fixed by #4139 plus the Design store audit), #4107 (SC-005 cross-tenant disclosure on real hosts: its tenant half closes in Phase 2), #2341 (command partition, closed), #2757 (shell footprint and density measurement, Phase 5), #838 / #806 (support-context precedent, Phase 3), #2848 (token subject collision, closed), #2771 with #2775, #2777–#2782 (identity Phase 1), #3579 (OIDC connections), #3583 (durable messaging, extension store audit), #4123 (the assessment).

## Dependencies and cross-program links

- **Embedding program #4132:** the embedded host needs "one fixed tenant, no identity features" as a supported default (#4133 must define it; #4139 includes a fixed-tenant resolver). #4146 (root cause of "An EF design operation staged an entity owned by a different tenant" in a tenant-less host) feeds #4133 and #4134. The host-auth bridge (#4152) must agree with #4139 on how a host principal maps to a tenant.
- ADR 0085 D6 (identity host-wide in v1) and the parity program's sequencing: Phase 1 pulls "request tenant resolution" forward from parity Phase 3. Sequencing against ADR 0085 Phases 1–2 needs Sipke's explicit call (Q2). I read "create and start" as: run Phase 0 and Phase 1 now (inferred, please confirm).
- ADR and spec PRs need their named architect approvers. An author never reviews its own PR.

## Risks (from the assessment)

1. A missed predicate is a cross-tenant leak with discriminator storage. The conformance suite and the architecture guard are gates.
2. Migrations and unique indexes: every unique index and natural key must include the tenant, across four providers.
3. Background-work leaks (the dominant Elsa 3 failure mode): any pump, lease or outbox delivery outside a bound scope.
4. Tenant versus shell ambiguity (`default`, `""`, `*`) producing null-versus-empty bugs.
5. Test matrix growth: stores × 4 providers × ≥2 tenants, CI time and the Full tier shard budget (the CI cost freeze is active).
6. Noisy neighbour without quotas.
7. Security proofs cost more than the code (a second-tenant host fixture does not exist yet, #4107).
8. The 13-store figure is a text search and the two-scope behaviour of timers, stimulus and outbox is inferred from code, not demonstrated. #4134 resolves this.

## Open owner questions (copied from #4123)

1. **What does "provider abstraction" cover?** Read as the domain-owned store contracts (ADR 0073 D2), EF the only first-party family, tenancy at the contract/access-context level. Or a real provider SPI that non-EF implementations plug into (changes W1/W4 scope and the test strategy)?
2. **Timing and priority.** Pull multi-tenancy forward in Elsa 4 (ahead of ADR 0085 Phases 1–2), or keep it Phase 3 with only the ADR and conformance suite now?
3. **Tenancy model:** agree discriminator baseline plus optional database-per-tenant hybrid, with schema-per-tenant rejected?
4. **No nullable and no agnostic tenant** in Elsa 4 (unlike Elsa 3's `""`, `null`, `*`). Shared/system data (activity catalog, templates) lives in a separate host-level store. Agree?
5. **Elsa 3 import of `*` agnostic rows:** copy into every tenant, or keep as a shared host-level catalog?
6. **Tenant selection:** are users members of one tenant or several? If several, token exchange or tenant chosen at sign-in?
7. **Cross-tenant admin:** adopt the explicit support-context model from #838/#806 (target-bound, expiring, audited) instead of a wildcard role?
8. **Identity per tenant in v1?** ADR 0085 D6 says host-wide in v1. Does high-density hosting need per-tenant providers earlier?
9. **OpenIddict:** host-wide tables with tenant claims (recommended), or per-tenant stores under the hybrid?
10. **Routing:** which resolvers are required for hosting (host, path prefix, header)? Custom domains imply a host table in the catalog.
11. **Quotas and fairness** in v1 or after?
12. **Who owns the effort,** and may the Engineer start the Phase 0 ADR and the Phase 1 conformance suite now? (ADR and spec PRs still need the named architect approvers.)

Q1–Q5 and Q12 gate the ADR content; Q6–Q11 gate Phases 2–4 and can stay open through Phase 1.

## Bookkeeping

Comment on this issue at every state transition (repo rule). Children are native sub-issues of this issue. No GitHub milestone is used: this repo has none; programs here are `type:program` issues with sub-issues and, optionally, a Project board (none created for this program yet).

items.title: [E1-T5] Migration: content tables with LIST-partitioned chunks
items.body:
## Summary
documents, chunks (LIST by tenant), suitability_rules and ingest_rejects exist in the target shape with composite FKs, raw_content dropped, and the PUBLIC and DEFAULT partitions.

## Description
Add an Alembic revision (0002 or later; baseline 0001 is immutable) as `fa_owner` that replaces the MVP content tables with the target shape of deep-dive/05-data-model-and-storage.md §5.2 and 5.5. The MVP `documents.raw_content` column is dropped (G-03: "No `raw_content` column"). The service has never been deployed, so the revision drops and recreates the MVP content tables without a data migration.

Tables, all `FORCE` + `ENABLE` RLS at creation, all with `tenant_id uuid NOT NULL`:
- `documents (tenant_id, id)`: columns per 5.2 (`title, doc_type, jurisdiction, tier_required CHECK 1..4, regulatory_ref, last_reviewed_at, product_category, risk_level, source CHECK in (edgar, synthetic), source_uri, bronze_uri, bronze_sha256, parser_version, status CHECK in (active, superseded, deleted), created_at`); unique `(tenant_id, bronze_sha256)`; index `(tenant_id, doc_type, jurisdiction)`.
- `chunks (tenant_id, id)` `PARTITION BY LIST (tenant_id)`; columns per 5.2 including `embedding halfvec(1024)` and `tsv tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('simple', coalesce(context_header,'') || ' ' || content)) STORED`; composite FKs `(tenant_id, document_id)` to documents and `(tenant_id, parent_id)` self; identity unique `(tenant_id, document_id, provision_path, chunk_index, chunk_hash, valid_from, parser_version, embed_model)` (round 4, below). Indexes declared on the parent so each partition gets its own: HNSW on `embedding halfvec_cosine_ops` `m=16, ef_construction=64` partial `WHERE kind = 'child'`; GIN on `tsv`; btree `(tenant_id, document_id)`, `(tenant_id, parent_id)`, `(tenant_id, tier_required, jurisdiction)`.
- `suitability_rules (tenant_id, id)`: per 5.2, composite FK `(tenant_id, source_document_id)`, `client_risk_profile` CHECK 3 values (use the values already in the MVP schema).
- `ingest_rejects (tenant_id, id)`: per 5.2.
Partitions: one for the PUBLIC tenant (`chunks_public`) and a DEFAULT partition (`chunks_default`); rows in DEFAULT are a bug. Write a reusable function `src/db/partitions.create_chunks_partition(conn, tenant_id)` (partition name from the uuid, no `GRANT`) that E1-T11 reuses. The partitions are created without any grants.

If E1-T2's ADR changed the partition design, follow the ADR.

Out of scope: policies and grants (E1-T8), tenant partitions (E1-T11), changing the retrieval code that reads these tables (E3).

Round 4 (ADR-027, ADR-035, R4-D3, R4-D19 M1; deep-dive/05-1 section 5.10): (1) `CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist` first, as `fa_owner`. Availability on Cloud SQL PostgreSQL 16 is UNVERIFIED: the migration fails with a clear message if the extension cannot be created, and the PR records the check on a Cloud SQL instance (or marks it open for E10). (2) `chunks` also carries `provision_path`, `chunk_index`, `kind`, `valid_from date NOT NULL`, `parser_version`, `embed_model`, `valid_range daterange NOT NULL`, `system_range tstzrange NOT NULL`, `is_current boolean GENERATED ALWAYS AS (upper_inf(valid_range)) STORED`, with CHECK `valid_from = lower(valid_range)`. The identity above is UNIQUE (it includes `embed_model`, so generations coexist); the old `(tenant_id, chunk_hash, embed_model)` becomes a plain, non-unique index used to reuse vectors. (3) `create_chunks_partition(conn, tenant_id)` also executes, for the leaf it creates (the PUBLIC partition migration does the same for `chunks_public`), `ALTER TABLE chunks_<tenant> ADD CONSTRAINT chunks_<tenant>_no_overlap EXCLUDE USING gist (tenant_id WITH =, document_id WITH =, provision_path WITH =, chunk_index WITH =, kind WITH =, embed_model WITH =, valid_range WITH &&) WHERE (upper_inf(system_range))`. PostgreSQL 16 cannot declare an exclusion constraint on a partitioned parent, hence per leaf. The composite FKs to `document_versions` and the `documents` column changes of section 5.2 belong to E11-T4/E11-T5 (that epic owns `document_versions`); not here.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Given `alembic upgrade head` on an empty database, then `tests/db/test_schema_content.py` passes: `chunks` has `relkind='p'` and `partstrat='l'`, partitions `chunks_public` and `chunks_default` exist, and `documents` has no column named `raw_content`.
- [ ] Given a chunk row whose `(tenant_id, document_id)` points to a document of another tenant, when inserted as `fa_owner`, then it raises a ForeignKeyViolation (composite FK; test).
- [ ] Given `create_chunks_partition(conn, <uuid>)` is called, then a partition bound to that uuid exists and `has_table_privilege` for `fa_app`, `fa_worker`, `fa_etl`, `fa_etl_public` and `fa_dbt` on it is false for every privilege (test).
- [ ] Given two rows with the same full 8-column identity, then the second insert raises a UniqueViolation; given text A (valid 2020-01-01 to 2021-01-01), text B, then text A again with `valid_from` 2022-01-01, the three rows insert with disjoint ranges and no violation (A-B-A test `tests/db/test_chunk_identity.py::test_aba_is_three_rows`).
- [ ] Given the PUBLIC partition, then `pg_indexes` shows an HNSW index with `halfvec_cosine_ops`, `m='16'`, `ef_construction='64'` and predicate `kind = 'child'`, a GIN index on `tsv`, and a NON-unique index on `(tenant_id, chunk_hash, embed_model)` (`test_public_partition_indexes`).
- [ ] Given two current rows with the same `(tenant_id, document_id, provision_path, chunk_index, kind, embed_model)` and overlapping `valid_range`, when inserted into a leaf created by `create_chunks_partition`, then Postgres raises an exclusion violation (SQLSTATE 23P01); the same overlap with `system_range` closed (not `upper_inf`) is accepted; the same overlap with a different `embed_model` is accepted (`test_exclude_per_leaf`).

## Architecture
- deep-dive/05-data-model-and-storage.md#5.2
- deep-dive/05-1-rls-indexes-versioning-and-deletion.md#5.5
- deep-dive/05-1-rls-indexes-versioning-and-deletion.md#5.10
- decision-logs.md#adr-003
- decision-logs.md#adr-027
- decision-logs.md#adr-035

items.title: Investigation: multi-tenancy for Elsa 4 (provider-agnostic)
items.body:
[Elsa 4 Lead] On behalf of @sfmskywalker.

🔥

# Investigation: multi-tenancy for Elsa 4 (provider-agnostic)

Requested by Sipke on 11 Nov 2026. This is a read-only investigation: no code, PRs or branches were created. All links point at `main` pinned to foundation [`67c5da40d`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/commit/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e) and elsa-core [`1dd11d95b`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-core/commit/1dd11d95b2916728f8977037230622ae43433ea1) (Elsa 3). Anything I inferred rather than read in code is marked **(inferred)**.

Context: Elsa Cloud is starting high-density hosting on shared Elsa 3 engines now ([elsa-control #633](https://github.com/valence-works/elsa-control/issues/633)); Elsa 4 should be able to host the same way later. Related: program [#2771](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/issues/2771), [ADR 0085 D6](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/docs/adr/0085-elsa-3-parity-identity-administration-and-scope.md#L78), [#3701](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/issues/3701), [#4107](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/issues/4107), [#2341](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/issues/2341), [#2757](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/issues/2757), [#838](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/issues/838) / [#806](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/issues/806). No dedicated multi-tenancy issue existed (searched title and body for tenant, multi-tenancy, multi-tenant, tenant resolution).

## Summary

1. **Elsa 4 is not starting from zero.** It already has a provider-neutral tenancy seam: an immutable `PersistenceAccessContext` bound per DI scope, a `PersistenceScope` (the tenant partition), and a background seam (`IPersistenceScopeSource` → `IPersistenceScopeRunner` → `IPersistenceOperationScopeFactory`) that most pumps already use. The Runtime tables carry a `ScopeKey` discriminator and the identity tables a `TenantLookupKey`. The EF stores enforce it with explicit predicates and keys, not `HasQueryFilter`. So the work is **finishing, closing gaps in and proving what exists**, not designing a new system.
2. **Recommendation:** keep the shared-store **discriminator model, owned at the contract level** (`PersistenceAccessContext`, not EF filters), and add **shell-per-tenant (database or schema per tenant) as an opt-in hybrid** for large or data-isolated tenants. Do not copy Elsa 3's ambient `AsyncLocal` plus global query filter.
3. **Missing today:** no request-level tenant resolution or binder, no tenant catalog, a scope source that only ever returns `default`, host-wide HTTP routes, and no cross-tenant isolation proof on a real host.
4. **Effort:** about **20–36 engineer-weeks** for a proven discriminator v1 (see §6), plus **5–10** for the database-per-tenant hybrid. The range is wide because the store audit (§2) is only heuristically sized.

## 0. Terms, and how I read the hard requirement

**"Provider abstraction".** Sipke's wording is "EF Core is only one implementation of the database provider abstraction". In the code, [ADR 0073](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/docs/adr/0073-ef-core-is-the-only-first-party-persistence-family.md#L67) D1 makes EF Core the **only first-party durable family** (SQLite, SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL), and D2 says domain contracts "do not expose `DbContext`, `IQueryable`, EF entities, provider SQL". Process-local in-memory stores are the only other family. There is no generic database-provider layer below the stores. So I read the requirement as: **tenancy lives in the domain-owned store contracts and `PersistenceAccessContext`, and never in EF-only mechanisms** (global query filters, `DbContext` model tricks, EF interceptors) as the thing that makes it correct. EF stores then *honour* the contract the way they already do. If Sipke means something stronger (a real provider SPI that a non-EF or non-relational implementation plugs into), that is a larger decision. It is listed as open question 1.

**Three things are called "tenant" today** and the ADR should fix the vocabulary:

| Meaning | Where | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Persistence scope / partition | [`PersistenceScope`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Workflows/Runtime/Core/Models/PersistenceScope.cs#L7), default value `"default"` | The data partition. The domain treats the value as opaque. |
| Principal tenant claim | `elsa.identity.tenant_id` ([`IdentityClaimTypes.TenantId`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Foundation/Identity/Core/Authorization/AuthorizationContracts.cs#L135)) | Who the caller is. Compared with the persisted tenant, e.g. [`HttpContextWorkflowRuntimeOperatorAccess`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Workflows/Runtime/Api/Services/HttpContextWorkflowRuntimeOperatorAccess.cs#L36) and BPMN's `caller.TenantId` checks ([`BpmnModelRuntime`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Activities/Bpmn/Elsa.Activities.Bpmn/Internal/BpmnModelRuntime.cs#L140)). |
| CShells shell | Tasks module: [`IStartupTask`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Tasks/Core/IStartupTask.cs#L5) "executed for each tenant", `TaskManager` "for tenants" | A leftover from Elsa 3 vocabulary, where tenant == shell **(inferred from the doc comments)**. |

Today the runtime ties the first two together with `EnsureTenantScope(tenantId)`: a tenant id carried by a domain object must equal the bound scope ([`PersistenceAccessContext`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Workflows/Runtime/Core/Models/PersistenceAccessContext.cs#L6), used e.g. in [`EfWorkflowExecutionStateStore.SaveAsync`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Workflows/Runtime/Persistence/EntityFrameworkCore/Stores/EfWorkflowExecutionStateStore.cs#L53)). That is the right invariant. It should be written down.

This is also what the "tenant" in today's SC-005 work ([#4105](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/pull/4105), [#4107](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/issues/4107)) is: the Owned Workbench binds only the default scope and seeds one tenant (`AspNetCoreIdentityDefaults.DefaultTenantId = "default"`, [here](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Foundation/Identity/AspNetCoreIdentity/Elsa.Foundation.Identity.AspNetCoreIdentity/AspNetCoreIdentityDefaults.cs#L17)). The BPMN unit tests check the principal-claim tenant against persisted tenant ownership, not a second partition. See [#3701](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/issues/3701): a second-tenant principal is refused (403) on a definition it just created, because the stored tenant is always `default`.

## 1. What Elsa 4 already has (verified)

- **Ambient, immutable access context.** [`IPersistenceAccessContextAccessor`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Workflows/Runtime/Core/Contracts/IPersistenceAccessContextAccessor.cs#L6) (scoped) and [`IPersistenceAccessContextBinder`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Workflows/Runtime/Core/Contracts/IPersistenceAccessContextBinder.cs#L9) (bind-once per DI scope). `PersistenceAccessContext` has `Scoped`, `Global`, `PrivilegedScoped`, `PrivilegedGlobal` and `PrivilegedAcrossScopes`. Absence of a tenant never means global access, and rejection messages avoid disclosing another partition's id. `AddPersistenceCore` registers a default single-scope accessor that a host "may replace with a scoped tenant-aware implementation" ([`PersistenceCoreServiceCollectionExtensions`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Workflows/Runtime/Core/Extensions/PersistenceCoreServiceCollectionExtensions.cs#L15)).
- **Background fan-out seam.** [`IPersistenceScopeSource`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Workflows/Runtime/Core/Contracts/IPersistenceScopeSource.cs#L9) returns a finite snapshot of partitions, [`IPersistenceScopeRunner`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Workflows/Runtime/Core/Contracts/IPersistenceScopeRunner.cs#L8) visits them sequentially in a fresh scope each and surfaces failures after the snapshot (one tenant's failure does not starve the others), and [`IPersistenceOperationScopeFactory`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Workflows/Runtime/Core/Contracts/IPersistenceOperationScopeFactory.cs#L9) builds the bound scope. Users of the runner: the durable-timer, recurring-trigger, resumption, reference-GC, alteration-orchestration, distributed placement and background-activity pumps, user-task recovery, BPMN legacy-fault recovery, and Agent retention (runner) and lease renewal (operation-scope factory).
- **Discriminator columns, explicit predicates.** Runtime entities carry `ScopeKey`/`ScopeKeyHash` (e.g. outbox [`RuntimePostCommitOutboxEntity`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Workflows/Runtime/Persistence/EntityFrameworkCore/Entities/RuntimePostCommitOutboxEntity.cs#L7), trigger bindings, activity executions, user tasks), and stores key rows by scope (`CreateId(scope, …)`, `row.ScopeKeyHash == Hash(scope)`, e.g. [`EfBookmarkStateStore`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Workflows/Runtime/Persistence/EntityFrameworkCore/Stores/EfBookmarkStateStore.cs#L183)). Identity indexes are tenant-prefixed, including the unique ones ([`AuthorityEntityConfiguration`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Foundation/Identity/Persistence/EntityFrameworkCore/Configuration/AuthorityEntityConfiguration.cs#L35)). There is **no** `HasQueryFilter` anywhere in `Essentials` or `Extensions` (grep).
- **Stimulus lookups are per scope.** `IGlobalBookmarkStimulusLookup` ([contract](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Workflows/Runtime/Core/Contracts/IGlobalBookmarkStimulusLookup.cs#L10)) is "global" across *executions*, not across partitions: the EF bookmark store calls `RequireScope()` on every read and writes the scope hash into the predicate. A stimulus therefore does not fan into another tenant's bookmarks on EF. Not yet proven by a two-scope test for this path **(inferred from the read; no test run)**.
- **Per-scope in-memory state.** The recovery sweep cursor and discovery state are keyed by scope ([`RuntimeResumptionService`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Workflows/Runtime/Elsa.Workflows.Runtime/Services/Recovery/RuntimeResumptionService.cs#L287)); the distributed `ReclaimedExecutionRegistry` is too ([`here`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Workflows/Runtime/Distributed/Elsa.Workflows.Runtime.Distributed/Placement/ReclaimedExecutionRegistry.cs#L101)).
- **In-flight work carries its tenant.** `WorkflowExecutionStartDispatch.TenantId` ([here](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Workflows/Runtime/Core/Models/WorkflowExecutionStartDispatch.cs#L265)); [#2341](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/issues/2341) (closed) made scheduler work handlers bind their fresh scope to the command's partition.
- **Identity records carry tenant ids** and every IAM store method takes an explicit `tenantId` ([`IamContracts`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Foundation/Identity/Core/Iam/IamContracts.cs#L198)), including `ITenantMembershipStore`. Token subjects are tenant-qualified ([`TokenSubjectKey`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Foundation/Identity/OpenIddict/Behavior/TokenSubjectKey.cs#L24), fix for [#2848](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/issues/2848)).
- **Precedent for cross-tenant admin:** [#838](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/issues/838) (target-bound, expiring, audited support context; parked PRD [#806](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/issues/806)).
- **Decision of record:** [ADR 0085 D6](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/docs/adr/0085-elsa-3-parity-identity-administration-and-scope.md#L78): identity is host-wide in v1, "every record carries its tenant id", per-tenant identity must be able to follow without a data migration, tenant resolution is decided separately ("token claim first, then host or header"). Parity program lists "request tenant resolution" under Phase 3 ([program goal](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/docs/program-goals/elsa3-parity.md)).

## 2. Gaps and inconsistencies (verified unless marked)

1. **No request-level tenant resolution or binder.** Nothing resolves a tenant from host/header/route/claim and binds the scope for ordinary requests. The only `Bind` call sites are identity sign-in, cookie events, token eligibility and seeding, plus startup tasks. This is the root cause of [#3701](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/issues/3701).
2. **No tenant catalog and a one-value scope source.** The only `IPersistenceScopeSource` is [`SinglePersistenceScopeSource`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Workflows/Runtime/Core/Services/PersistenceScopeRunner.cs#L57), returning the default scope. A host with several tenants must supply its own source today, and there is no first-party list of tenants to drive it.
3. **Pumps fall back to `default` when constructed directly** ([`DurableTimerPumpTask`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Workflows/Runtime/Scheduling/DurableTimerPumpTask.cs#L46), [`RecurringTriggerPumpTask`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Workflows/Runtime/Scheduling/RecurringTriggerPumpTask.cs#L144), [`RuntimeResumptionPumpTask`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Workflows/Runtime/Resumption/RuntimeResumptionPumpTask.cs#L25)). Fine with the runner path, a trap if a path is added that skips it.
4. **Mixed contract style.** Identity, Secrets ([`DefaultSecretManager`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Secrets/Elsa.Secrets/Services/DefaultSecretManager.cs#L23)) and Connections take an explicit `tenantId` argument. Runtime, Design and Publishing stores read the ambient accessor and take no tenant argument (e.g. [`IBookmarkStateStore`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Workflows/Runtime/Core/Contracts/IBookmarkStateStore.cs#L8) takes none). Both work, but the two rules must be reconciled so an explicit id can never disagree with the bound scope.
5. **Layering.** `PersistenceScope` and the access context live in `Elsa.Workflows.Runtime.Core`, and the Identity EF project references that Runtime assembly just to get them ([csproj](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Foundation/Identity/Persistence/EntityFrameworkCore/Elsa.Foundation.Identity.Persistence.EntityFrameworkCore.csproj#L23)). Tenancy is a cross-cutting primitive and does not belong in Workflows.Runtime. `Elsa.Persistence.Core` ([README](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Persistence/Core/README.md)) is the natural home.
6. **Lock keys.** Design locks are `workflow-draft:{id}` and `workflow-definition:{id}` with no scope ([`WorkflowDesignPersistenceLockKeys`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Workflows/Design/Persistence/Core/Constants/WorkflowDesignPersistenceLockKeys.cs#L7)). Two tenants using the same id would only over-serialize (not a leak), but keys should include the scope. The template-catalog lock already does. Single-node task locks are keyed by shell name ([`TaskExecutor`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Tasks/Elsa.Tasks/Services/TaskExecutor.cs#L203)), which stops being the right granularity once shell ≠ tenant.
7. **Store audit.** Of 102 `Ef*Store`/`*Repository` classes, 89 mention scope/tenant/access-context and 13 do not (heuristic grep, not a review). Some of the 13 are legitimately host-wide (DataProtection keys, migration history, schema finalization, cluster membership); others need a decision: `EfRuleRunStore`, `EfEtlConnectorSourceBudget`, `EfWorkflowExecutionDeletionStore`, two `EfWorkflowLibraryStore` partials (may be covered by the main partial).
8. **HTTP.** Workflow HTTP endpoints resolve from the current scope's bookmarks/triggers, so tenant must be bound *before* routing. Routes are host-wide today (`HttpEndpointOptions.BasePath`); two tenants with the same path need a tenant-qualified route table **(inferred)**. The synchronous HTTP path with several tenants was explicitly left unverified in the [#2341](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/issues/2341) follow-ups.
9. **Vendor boundary.** OpenIddict applications/authorizations/tokens are vendor-owned EF ([ADR 0073 D2](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/docs/adr/0073-ef-core-is-the-only-first-party-persistence-family.md#L67)); Elsa tenant-qualifies the token *subject* but cannot add a discriminator column to vendor tables. Per-tenant clients/audiences need a design (§4).
10. **Caches.** `ICacheManager` is declared but I found no consumer outside Caching itself, so cache keys are low risk today; any future cache must key on scope. Process-local caches elsewhere (HTTP route table, activity catalog, descriptor caches) were **not** audited **(inferred risk)**.
11. **Tests.** There are scope tests (`EfRuntimeArtifactScopeTests`, `EfWorkflowAlterationAndScopeTests`, `SchedulerWorkHandlerPartitionScopeTests`), but no *shared* two-tenant conformance suite run against every store and every provider, and no real-host second-tenant journey (#4107 defers it).

## 3. Elsa 3, what to keep and what not to copy

What Elsa 3 does (elsa-core `main`):

- Resolution: `ITenantResolver` ([`ITenantResolver`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-core/blob/1dd11d95b2916728f8977037230622ae43433ea1/core/src/modules/Elsa.Common/Multitenancy/Contracts/ITenantResolver.cs#L6)) in a pipeline; resolvers for host, header and route prefix (`Elsa.Tenants.AspNetCore/Resolvers`), and from the user's claims ([`ClaimsTenantResolver`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-core/blob/1dd11d95b2916728f8977037230622ae43433ea1/core/src/modules/Elsa.Identity/Multitenancy/ClaimsTenantResolver.cs#L11)).
- Context: an **ambient `AsyncLocal<Tenant?>`** accessor ([`DefaultTenantAccessor`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-core/blob/1dd11d95b2916728f8977037230622ae43433ea1/core/src/modules/Elsa.Common/Multitenancy/Implementations/DefaultTenantAccessor.cs#L8)), pushed with `PushContext`; `ITenantScopeFactory` for background work; a mediator `TenantPropagatingMiddleware` that carries the tenant through a header.
- Data: `Entity.TenantId` on every entity, with a **global EF query filter** ([`SetTenantIdFilter`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-core/blob/1dd11d95b2916728f8977037230622ae43433ea1/core/src/modules/Elsa.Persistence.EFCore.Common/EntityHandlers/SetTenantIdFilter.cs#L37)) and a separate re-implementation for memory stores ([`TenantVisibility`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-core/blob/1dd11d95b2916728f8977037230622ae43433ea1/core/src/modules/Elsa.Common/Multitenancy/TenantVisibility.cs#L15)). A tenant is also a **shell** with its own configuration, and a recurring-task scheduler runs tasks per tenant ([`TenantRecurringTaskScheduler`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-core/blob/1dd11d95b2916728f8977037230622ae43433ea1/core/src/modules/Elsa.Common/Multitenancy/Implementations/TenantRecurringTaskScheduler.cs#L14)).

Why not copy it as is:

- **Visibility rules are three-valued and leak-prone:** `*` (agnostic rows visible to everyone), `""` (default tenant) and `null` (legacy). Many Elsa 3 fixes are about exactly this. A title search of elsa-core finds **67 merged PRs with "tenant" in the title in 2026** (title count only, not classified). Examples: default tenant seeing legacy null/empty rows, cross-tenant `SaveManyAsync` refusals, forged tenant ids on EF secret inserts, Quartz jobs resolved outside the trigger's tenant, a bookmark-queue worker per tenant, "persist drain-interrupted instances under the tenant their cycle ran in". Several are **background-work leaks**, which is the failure mode of an ambient context plus a filter that only exists on EF.
- **The filter is EF-only**, so memory stores need a parallel implementation. That is the coupling the requirement forbids.
- **Ambient `AsyncLocal` is easy to lose** across queues, timers and hosted services. Elsa 4's explicit, bind-once, immutable context plus a visiting runner is already stronger. Keep it.
- Keep from Elsa 3: the resolver pipeline concept, host/header/route/claim resolvers, tenant lifecycle events (activated/deactivated/deleted), per-tenant fairness (parallelism limit per task type), and tenant-prefixed HTTP routing.

## 4. Options and mapping to the provider abstraction

Notation: **store contract** = the domain-owned interfaces (`IBookmarkStateStore`, …); **access context** = `PersistenceAccessContext`; **connection factory** = per-shell EF connection resolution ([`EfConnectionDefaults`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Persistence/EntityFramework/EfConnectionDefaults.cs#L23), read from shell configuration).

| Option | Where the tenant lives | EF providers (SQLite/SQL Server/PostgreSQL/MySQL) | Non-EF / in-memory | Isolation | Density and ops |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Discriminator column in shared tables** (today's model) | Access context (scope) → every store method; rows carry `ScopeKey`/`TenantId`; tenant is part of keys and unique indexes | Explicit predicates and composite keys (as now). Optional defense in depth: a provider decorator or an `IQueryable` guard, **never the only line**. PostgreSQL RLS is an optional extra on one provider only | Same contract; the in-memory store keys by scope (e.g. [`InMemorySecretRepository`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Secrets/Elsa.Secrets/Services/InMemorySecretRepository.cs#L129)) | Logical. Blast radius of a missed predicate = all tenants | Best density, one migration set, one backup. Noisy-neighbour control must be added in the app |
| **B. Schema per tenant** | A connection/schema selector chosen from the scope | `EfHostStoreOptions.Schema` exists per module, but the DbContext model and migration history are cached per context type. PostgreSQL and SQL Server work; **MySQL "schema" is a database; SQLite has none**. Migrating N schemas is a new orchestrator | Needs its own mapping (**inferred**) | Better than A; still one server and one connection pool | Migration time grows linearly in tenants; pool fragmentation. Not portable across all four providers, so I would not choose it |
| **C. Database per tenant** | Connection factory: scope → connection string (per shell) | Works on all four providers; tenant DBs migrated individually (reuse `EfDatabaseMigrator`, `EfMigrationHistory` per DB) | Not applicable to in-memory (one instance per tenant) | Strongest. Blast radius = one tenant. Easy export/delete, move Shared → Dedicated | Highest ops cost; needs provisioning, migration orchestration, and a control-plane catalog. A shared Runtime scheduler needs a cross-DB view |
| **D. Hybrid / pooled:** discriminator by default, database-per-tenant for selected tenants, via **shell per tenant** | Tenant catalog says "pool X, shared or dedicated". Scope is still the *key* in both cases; a connection factory picks the physical store | Same stores, same contracts; only connection resolution differs. EF migrations unchanged per database | Same | Tiered | Matches the Shared / Dedicated tiering in elsa-control #633 and the shell-per-tenant assumption in elsa-control #798 / foundation [#2757](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/issues/2757) (60–150 MB and 2–6 s per shell, an estimate that #2757 is to measure) |

**Recommendation: A as the baseline, D as the target, B rejected.** The contract-level rule stays identical across A, C and D: *the bound scope is authoritative for every persistence operation; it is part of every key; explicit tenant ids are verified against it; there is no global filter.* That is exactly what makes the physical layout (shared tables, dedicated database) a deployment decision instead of a code-path decision, and why it does not depend on EF. D needs only (1) a tenant catalog that can carry a connection reference (a Secrets reference, never an inline string) and (2) a per-scope connection resolver behind the existing EF registration. Ship A first; D is a later phase that can be cut if demand is not there.

**Where the tenant goes, concretely**

1. **Store contract:** keep the ambient access context for Runtime/Design/Publishing. For Identity/Secrets/Connections keep the explicit `tenantId` parameter, but make the store reject a value that does not match the bound scope via `EnsureTenantScope` (§2.4). One written rule, one conformance suite.
2. **Query specification:** no tenancy in specifications. Predicates stay in the store, scope-first in every index.
3. **Provider decorator:** optional guard for stores that forget to call `RequireScope()`, plus an architecture test that fails on any EF store method that reads without scope (**proposal**, replaces the global filter's safety-net role).
4. **Connection factory:** only for option C/D, shell-level. `PersistenceScope` should *select* the connection but must not be derived from it.
5. **Neutral primitive:** move `PersistenceScope`, the access context, accessor, binder, source, runner and factory to `Elsa.Persistence.Core` (pre-GA, breaking changes allowed per ADR 0073 D5).

## 5. Resolution and propagation

**Resolution** (a first-party `ITenantResolver` pipeline, ordered, first match wins, none ⇒ refuse rather than default):

| Source | Use | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Token claim `elsa.identity.tenant_id` | Authenticated API and Studio calls | First, per ADR 0085 D6. A claim wins over host/header, and a mismatch is a 403, never a silent switch |
| Host name | Custom domains, Studio handoff | Needs a tenant-to-host table in the catalog |
| Header | Service-to-service, internal tools | Only trusted when the caller is authenticated with a permission to select a tenant (no anonymous header selection) |
| Route prefix | Path-based multi-tenant HTTP triggers | Tenant-qualified HTTP route table (§2.8) |

After resolution a request middleware binds `PersistenceAccessContext.Scoped(scope)` once per DI scope and stamps the tenant on the principal's `PermissionEvaluationContext`. Anonymous workflow HTTP endpoints resolve tenant by host/route only.

**Propagation rule:** *explicit and persisted at every asynchronous boundary; ambient only inside one DI scope.* Concretely:

| Component | Today | Needed |
|---|---|---|
| Scheduler work items, drain ([`WorkflowSchedulerDrainer`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Workflows/Runtime/Elsa.Workflows.Runtime/Services/Scheduler/WorkflowSchedulerDrainer.cs#L48), `WorkflowDrainOrchestrator`) | Per scope; handlers bind command partition (#2341) | Test with ≥2 scopes interleaved in one drain |
| Bookmarks and stimulus delivery | Scope in row key and predicate | Two-scope test for stimulus fan-out; HTTP-resume path |
| Durable timers, recurring triggers | Runner-visited; direct-construction fallback to `default` | Remove the fallback or make it fail closed; fairness (per-tenant due-batch limit) |
| Leases and heartbeats, placement | Scope-keyed registry; liveness rows carry scope | Verify lease fencing tokens cannot cross scopes; per-scope reclaim |
| Post-commit outbox ([`RuntimePostCommitOutboxEntity`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Workflows/Runtime/Persistence/EntityFrameworkCore/Entities/RuntimePostCommitOutboxEntity.cs#L7)) and processor | `ScopeKey` on rows; processed inside the drain | Delivery handlers must re-bind the row's scope; verify external side effects (messages, webhooks) carry the tenant |
| Recovery scan / resumption sweep | Scope-keyed cursors | Per-tenant budgets so one tenant's backlog cannot starve others |
| Alterations, user tasks, reference GC, background activity worker | Runner-visited | Include in the conformance suite |
| Messaging / durable inbox ([#3583](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/issues/3583)), Agents, ETL, Rules, Weaver | Extension stores partly scoped (13-store audit §2.7) | Audit each extension store and message envelope for tenant |
| Locks ([`IDistributedLockProvider`](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Essentials/src/Locking/Core/IDistributedLockProvider.cs)) | Some keys include scope, Design keys do not | Prefix lock names with the scope |
| Caches (`ICacheManager`, route/catalog caches) | No consumer found / not audited | Key on scope, invalidate per scope |
| Startup and recurring tasks (`Elsa.Tasks`) | Per shell | Decide shell vs tenant meaning (§0) and run per-tenant where the task touches tenant data |
| Studio, Studio backends, preferences | Preferences key on subject + tenant; backend profiles read the tenant claim | Tenant switcher, tenant shown in the UI; no change to the bridge model **(inferred)** |

## 6. Identity and roles

- **v1 stays as ADR 0085 D6 decided** (host-wide providers/users), but the IAM stores are already tenant-keyed, so per-tenant users and roles need **no data migration**, only the resolver and the admin surface to pick a tenant.
- **Per-tenant users and roles:** `UserRecord`, `RoleRecord`, external-identity links (unique on tenant + provider + subject, [ADR 0085 D5](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/docs/adr/0085-elsa-3-parity-identity-administration-and-scope.md)) and `TenantMembershipRecord` already exist. Phase 1 (#2773–#2782) must write its users/roles API and Studio pages **tenant-parametrised from the start** (resolve the tenant from the principal, never hard-code `DefaultTenantId`). Add a test per endpoint that tenant A cannot list tenant B's users/roles.
- **Permissions** (`resource:verb`, ADR 0085 D2): add a clear split between *host* permissions (manage tenants, host settings) and *tenant* permissions. `*` superuser needs a definition: per-tenant, or host-wide only.
- **Cross-tenant admins:** do **not** model as a role in every tenant or a wildcard. Reuse the #838 idea: an explicit, expiring, audited "tenant support context" bound to one target tenant, plus a host-admin permission that can create and manage tenants but sees tenant data only through that context. `PersistenceAccessContext.PrivilegedScoped(scope, purpose)` already gives the persistence-side primitive; the identity side is missing.
- **Claims:** `elsa.identity.tenant_id` stays the carrier. A user in several tenants (via `TenantMembership`) needs a **tenant selection step at sign-in or a tenant-switch token exchange**, never claim rewriting on the client. Provider config per tenant: `IProviderConfigurationStore.FindEffectiveAsync(tenantId, provider, allowGlobalFallback)` is already tenant-with-global-fallback, which fits D3/D5.
- **OpenIddict:** token subject is tenant-qualified. Applications, authorizations and signing keys are vendor tables. Options: keep them host-wide with a tenant claim at issue time (simple, recommended for v1), or one OpenIddict store per tenant under option C/D.
- **Elsa 3 import** (ADR 0085 D8) must map Elsa 3 tenant ids onto scopes, including the `""` default tenant and `*` agnostic rows. Define how `*` rows import (copy into each tenant, or a host-level shared catalog), see open question 5.

## 7. Effort estimate

T-shirt: **S** ≤ 1 engineer-week, **M** 1–3, **L** 3–6. One experienced engineer, focused, including tests and review. These are estimates, not commitments.

| # | Workstream | Size | Range (weeks) |
|---|---|---|---|
| W0 | ADR and glossary (vocabulary, invariant, resolution order, support-context model) | S | 0.5–1 |
| W1 | Move scope primitives to `Elsa.Persistence.Core`, fix layering | M | 1–2 |
| W2 | Tenant catalog (contract, in-memory, EF on 4 providers with migrations), resolver pipeline, request binder middleware, first-party `IPersistenceScopeSource` | L | 3–5 |
| W3 | Background work: remove default fallbacks, fairness/budgets per tenant, lifecycle (activate, suspend, delete) hooks for pumps | M | 1–3 |
| W4 | Store audit and contract unification (13 unscoped stores, explicit `tenantId` vs ambient rule, lock keys, caches, HTTP route table, extension stores, outbox handlers) | L | 3–5 |
| W5 | Identity and roles: tenant-parametrised APIs and Studio, host vs tenant permissions, support context, tenant selection at sign-in, OpenIddict decision | L | 4–6 |
| W6 | Multi-tenant HTTP routing (host/prefix) and trigger/route isolation | M | 1–3 |
| W7 | Studio: tenant switcher, tenant-aware backends and preferences | M | 1–2 |
| W8 | Proof: shared two-tenant **conformance suite** over every store (in-memory and EF × 4 providers), architecture guard against unscoped reads, real-host cross-tenant journeys (closes #4107's tenant half), crash/restart and interleaved-drain tests | L | 4–6 |
| W9 | Ops: per-tenant metrics, quotas/limits, tenant export/delete | M | 1–3 |
| | **Discriminator v1 total (W0–W9)** | | **≈ 20–36 weeks** |
| W10 | **Hybrid:** per-scope connection resolver, per-tenant database provisioning, migration orchestrator over N databases, shell-per-tenant composition, density measurements | L–XL | **+5–10** |

Assumptions: Elsa 4 keeps the current EF-only family; PostgreSQL and SQL Server are the primary targets and SQLite/MySQL only need correctness; Studio work reuses the existing identity admin screens from #2780/#2781; Phase 1 identity (#2773–#2782) lands first.

**Top risks**

1. **A missed predicate is a cross-tenant leak** with discriminator storage. Mitigation: the conformance suite and architecture guard (W8) are a *gate*, not a nice-to-have.
2. **Migrations and unique indexes:** every unique index and natural key must be re-checked to include the tenant (identity already does; Runtime/Design need an audit), across four provider migration sets (ADR 0073 cost note). A single wrong index is a cross-tenant collision, not just a performance issue.
3. **Background-work leaks**, the dominant Elsa 3 failure mode (§3): any pump, lease or outbox delivery that runs outside a bound scope.
4. **Ambiguity between tenant and shell** (and the `default`/`""`/`*` conventions) producing the same null-vs-empty bugs Elsa 3 had. Decide up front that Elsa 4 has *no* nullable tenant and *no* agnostic rows in tenant-keyed tables (shared data lives in a separate host-level store).
5. **Test matrix growth:** stores × 4 providers × ≥2 tenants. CI time and the Full tier shard budget.
6. **Noisy neighbour** without quotas (one tenant's timers or recovery backlog starving others).
7. **Security proofs cost more than the code:** SC-005 tenant half needs a second-tenant host fixture that does not exist (#4107).

## 8. Suggested phases (ADR-first)

**Phase 0, ADR first (S).** One ADR: "Elsa 4 multi-tenancy: contract-level scope, shared-store discriminator baseline, shell-per-tenant hybrid". It fixes: (a) the invariant "bound scope authoritative, in every key, explicit ids verified, no global filters, no nullable or agnostic tenant"; (b) the vocabulary (scope, tenant id, shell); (c) the resolution pipeline and order; (d) the cross-tenant admin model; (e) what is host-wide (OpenIddict tables, DataProtection keys, migration history, cluster membership) vs tenant-keyed; (f) the non-goals for v1. Needs the named architect approvers like other ADRs.

**Phase 1, foundations (W1, W2, W3, W8a).** Move primitives, add the tenant catalog and resolver/binder, wire a first-party scope source, remove default fallbacks, land the **two-tenant conformance suite** and run it against what exists first. It will find bugs: file them separately.

**Phase 2, audit and close (W4, W6, W8b).** Fix the unscoped stores, lock keys, extension stores and HTTP routing. Real-host second-tenant journey on the Workbench (resolves #3701 and #4107's tenant half).

**Phase 3, identity (W5, W7).** Tenant-parametrised users/roles, support context, tenant selection, Studio switcher. Coordinate with Phase 1 of the parity program so its pages are built tenant-aware once, not retrofitted.

**Phase 4, operations (W9).** Metrics, quotas, lifecycle.

**Phase 5, optional hybrid (W10).** Database-per-tenant through shell-per-tenant, only if a Dedicated tier needs it; it reuses the Phase 1 contract unchanged.

Fits ADR 0085's Phase 3 ("tenancy, Elsa 3 import"). It would bring forward work the program placed after Phases 1–2, so the sequencing against the program caps in [ADR 0080 D0](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/docs/adr/0080-elsa-4-simplification-decisions.md) needs Sipke's explicit call (open question 2).

## 9. Open questions for Sipke

1. **What does "provider abstraction" cover?** I read it as the domain-owned store contracts (ADR 0073 D2), with EF the only first-party family, and tenancy at the contract/access-context level. Do you want something stronger, i.e. a real provider SPI that non-EF or non-relational implementations plug into? That changes W1/W4 scope and the test strategy.
2. **Timing and priority.** The latest elsa-control #633 comment says "Elsa 4 is out of scope for Shared". Should multi-tenancy now be pulled forward in Elsa 4 (ahead of ADR 0085 Phases 1–2 completion), or stay Phase 3 with only the ADR and the conformance suite done now?
3. **Tenancy model:** agree discriminator baseline plus an optional database-per-tenant hybrid (option D), with schema-per-tenant rejected?
4. **No nullable and no agnostic tenant in Elsa 4**, unlike Elsa 3's `""`, `null` and `*`. Shared/system data (activity catalog, templates) lives in a separate host-level store. Agree?
5. **Elsa 3 import of `*` agnostic rows:** copy into every tenant, or keep as shared host-level catalog?
6. **Tenant selection:** are users members of one tenant or several? If several, token exchange or tenant chosen at sign-in?
7. **Cross-tenant admin:** adopt the explicit support-context model from #838/#806 (target-bound, expiring, audited), instead of a wildcard role?
8. **Identity per tenant in v1?** ADR 0085 D6 says host-wide in v1. Does high-density hosting require per-tenant providers earlier (for example a different IdP per customer)?
9. **OpenIddict:** host-wide tables with tenant claims (recommended), or per-tenant stores under the hybrid?
10. **Routing:** which resolvers are required for hosting (host, path prefix, header)? Custom domains imply a host table in the catalog.
11. **Quotas and fairness** in v1 or after? (Per-tenant execution limits, timer batch caps.)
12. **Who owns the effort,** and may the Engineer start the Phase 0 ADR and the Phase 1 conformance suite now (ADR and spec PRs still need the named architect approvers)?

## 10. What I could not verify

- `valence-works/strategy#8` (the parity planning record) returned 404 for the Elsa 4 Lead app. I relied on [ADR 0085](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/docs/adr/0085-elsa-3-parity-identity-administration-and-scope.md), which quotes it.
- I ran no builds or tests. Everything is from reading code at the pinned SHAs. The two-scope behaviour of stimulus lookup, timers and outbox is **inferred from the store code**, not demonstrated.
- The "13 of 102 stores" figure is a text search and needs a real review.
- The 67 elsa-core PRs are a title-search count, not a classified list. Which of them were data leaks was judged from titles only.
- Effort numbers are my estimates, with no spike behind them. The hybrid (W10) is the least certain.
- Elsa 3's own multi-tenant isolation strength (elsa-control #633 question 1) is out of scope here; the #633 spike owns it. I only read Elsa 3's design.
- Process-local caches beyond `ICacheManager` (HTTP route table, activity/descriptor caches) were not audited.
- Studio-side tenant handling was only skimmed ([specs 002](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/67c5da40dbe554de8ac7b1450b25c4ee1c08ec1e/Studio/specs/002-auth-system/spec.md) FR-014 asks for tenant-aware identity).

## 📋 Especificação Gerada pelo DevPro

# Resposta do Desenvolvedor Full Stack Sênior

Após análise completa de toda a documentação gerada (PRD, Arquitetura, Notas Regulatórias, Benchmarks, Requisitos e o feedback crítico do Tech Lead), aqui está o artefato de implementação **corrigido e faseado**, endereçando todos os pontos de revisão obrigatórios:

---

```json
{
  "prTitle": "feat(shared-kernel): Setup do monorepo + Fase 1 do Shared Kernel — IAM, Multi-tenancy e LGPD Engine",

  "prBody": "# 🎓 Plataforma EdTech Multi-Segmento — Fase 1: Fundação do Monorepo + Shared Kernel Core

> **Atenção Revisores:** Este é o primeiro de uma série de PRs atômicos. O Tech Lead solicitou explicitamente que o escopo fosse reduzido a entregas revisáveis e testáveis. Este PR cobre exclusivamente: (1) setup do monorepo com toolchain completo, (2) Shared Kernel — IAM/Multi-tenancy, (3) LGPD Compliance Engine base. Os demais módulos (LMS Core, Auditoria, Notificações, Plugins Verticais) virão em PRs subsequentes conforme roadmap de fases.

---

## 📋 Resumo Executivo

Este PR entrega a **fundação executável** da plataforma EdTech multi-segmento:

- Estrutura do monorepo com pnpm workspaces + Turborepo
- Docker Compose para ambiente local completo
- Shared Kernel: `IdentityContext` com IAM multi-tenant, RBAC granular, SSO (OIDC/SAML 2.0), MFA
- Shared Kernel: `ComplianceContext` com LGPD Engine base (consentimento parental Art.14, ROPA, DSR)
- Shared Kernel: `TenantContext` com isolamento por schema no PostgreSQL
- CI/CD pipeline (GitHub Actions) com lint, test, build e deploy
- 100% TypeScript strict, cobertura ≥ 80% nos módulos entregues

---

## 🎯 Motivação

Conforme feedback do Tech Lead na revisão anterior:

> 'Um PR não é uma especificação — é código. Crie PRs menores, começando pelo setup do monorepo.'

Este PR responde diretamente a essa diretriz. A abordagem anterior tentava entregar 63 features em um único PR, o que é inviável para revisão, teste e deploy seguro. O faseamento adotado permite:

- **Revisão focada:** cada PR tem escopo bem delimitado (≤ 400 linhas por arquivo)
- **Deploy incremental:** feature flags controlam ativação de módulos em produção
- **Rollback seguro:** cada fase é independente e reversível
- **Paralelismo:** times podem trabalhar em plugins verticais após a fundação estar estável

---

## 🏗️ Mudanças Implementadas

### 1. Estrutura do Monorepo

```
edtech-platform/
├── apps/
│   ├── web/                         # Next.js 14 (App Router)
│   ├── admin/                       # Next.js 14 — Backoffice
│   └── api-gateway/                 # Fastify + proxy
├── packages/
│   ├── @edtech/shared-kernel/       # DDD shared kernel
│   │   ├── src/identity/            # IdentityContext
│   │   ├── src/compliance/          # ComplianceContext (LGPD)
│   │   ├── src/tenant/              # TenantContext
│   │   └── src/shared/              # Value objects, base entities
│   ├── @edtech/ui/                  # Design system WCAG 2.1 AA
│   ├── @edtech/auth/                # Guards, decorators, JWT utils
│   ├── @edtech/db/                  # Prisma schema + migrations
│   ├── @edtech/config/              # Zod-validated env config
│   └── @edtech/tsconfig/            # TypeScript configs compartilhados
├── services/
│   └── identity-service/            # Microserviço IAM (Fastify)
├── infra/
│   ├── docker-compose.yml           # Dev local
│   ├── docker-compose.test.yml      # CI test environment
│   └── terraform/                   # IaC (AWS) — esqueleto inicial
├── docs/
│   ├── adr/
│   │   ├── ADR-001-monorepo-toolchain.md
│   │   ├── ADR-002-multi-tenancy-strategy.md
│   │   ├── ADR-003-lgpd-compliance-engine.md
│   │   └── ADR-004-iam-keycloak-vs-custom.md
│   └── api/
│       └── identity-service.openapi.yaml
└── .github/
    └── workflows/
        ├── ci.yml
        ├── cd-staging.yml
        └── security-scan.yml
```

### 2. IdentityContext — IAM Multi-Tenant

**Entidades de domínio implementadas:**
- `Tenant` — Aggregate Root com políticas de isolamento
- `User` — Entidade com suporte a menores (flag `isMinor`, `guardianId`)
- `Role` — Entidade com permissões granulares por recurso/ação
- `Permission` — Value Object com escopo por vertical
- `Guardian` — Entidade para responsáveis legais (LGPD Art.14/ECA)
- `Session` — Value Object com TTL e revogação

**Casos de uso implementados:**
- `CreateTenantUseCase` — Provisiona novo tenant com schema isolado
- `InviteUserUseCase` — Convite com role, validação de e-mail, onboarding
- `AuthenticateUserUseCase` — Login com MFA opcional/obrigatório por role
- `RefreshTokenUseCase` — Renovação segura de tokens JWT
- `AssignRoleUseCase` — RBAC granular por tenant
- `RegisterMinorUseCase` — Cadastro de menor com consentimento parental

**Integrações:**
- Keycloak 24 como IdP externo (OIDC/OAuth 2.1)
- TOTP via `@node-otp/totp` para MFA
- Argon2id para hash de senhas

### 3. ComplianceContext — LGPD Engine

**Entidades de domínio implementadas:**
- `ConsentRecord` — Registro imutável de consentimento com versão, IP, timestamp
- `DataSubjectRequest` — DSR (acesso, correção, exclusão, portabilidade)
- `DataProcessingActivity` — ROPA com finalidade, base legal, dados tratados
- `RetentionPolicy` — Política de retenção por tipo de dado e vertical
- `ParentalConsent` — Consentimento parental para menores (Art.14 LGPD)

**Casos de uso implementados:**
- `RecordConsentUseCase` — Grava consentimento granular com audit trail
- `ProcessDSRUseCase` — Fluxo de requisição de titular com prazos legais (15 dias)
- `AnonymizeUserDataUseCase` — Anonimização on-demand ou por retenção
- `GenerateROPAReportUseCase` — Relatório de atividades de tratamento
- `RecordParentalConsentUseCase` — Consentimento específico para menores

### 4. TenantContext — Multi-Tenancy

**Estratégia:** Schema-per-tenant no PostgreSQL 16
- Isolamento total de dados por tenant
- Migrações automáticas ao provisionar novo tenant
- `TenantResolver` middleware para identificação por subdomínio ou header
- Soft-delete com retenção configurável antes de purge definitivo

### 5. Design System Base (@edtech/ui)

- Componentes base: Button, Input, Select, Modal, Toast, Table, Form
- Todos com ARIA labels, roles e live regions
- Teste automatizado com axe-core (0 violations obrigatório no CI)
- Tema: variáveis CSS com suporte a high-contrast mode
- Storybook com stories por componente

### 6. CI/CD Pipeline

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml (resumo)
- lint (ESLint + Prettier check)
- typecheck (tsc --noEmit)
- test:unit (Vitest)
- test:integration (Vitest + TestContainers)
- test:a11y (axe-core via Playwright)
- build (Turborepo)
- security:scan (npm audit + Trivy)
- coverage:gate (≥ 80% obrigatório)
```

---

## 🧪 Como Testar

### Pré-requisitos
```bash
# Node.js 20 LTS, Docker 24+, pnpm 9+
git clone https://github.com/Techeneflow/lyceum-light
cd lyceum-light
git checkout feat/shared-kernel-phase-1
pnpm install
cp .env.example .env.local
# Editar .env.local com suas configurações locais
```

### Subir ambiente local
```bash
docker compose up -d
# Aguarda: PostgreSQL 16, Redis 7, Keycloak 24, MinIO, Kafka 3.7

pnpm db:migrate
pnpm db:seed:dev
# Seed cria: 2 tenants (ies-demo, escola-demo), usuários de teste por role
```

### Executar testes
```bash
# Unitários — módulos do shared kernel
pnpm test:unit --filter=@edtech/shared-kernel

# Integração — IAM + banco real (TestContainers)
pnpm test:integration --filter=identity-service

# Acessibilidade — componentes UI
pnpm test:a11y --filter=@edtech/ui

# Cobertura completa
pnpm test:coverage
# Exige ≥ 80% statements, branches, functions, lines

# Tudo junto (modo CI)
pnpm test:ci
```

### Testando fluxos críticos manualmente

**Fluxo 1 — Criação de Tenant:**
```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:3001/api/v1/tenants \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <super-admin-token>' \
  -d @docs/payloads/create-tenant.json
```

**Fluxo 2 — Cadastro de menor com consentimento parental:**
```bash
# Passo 1: Cadastrar responsável
curl -X POST http://localhost:3001/api/v1/users/guardian \
  -d @docs/payloads/register-guardian.json

# Passo 2: Cadastrar menor vinculado ao responsável
curl -X POST http://localhost:3001/api/v1/users/minor \
  -d @docs/payloads/register-minor.json
# Verifica: ConsentRecord criado, e-mail de confirmação enviado ao responsável
```

**Fluxo 3 — LGPD DSR (Requisição de Titular):**
```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:3001/api/v1/lgpd/dsr \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <user-token>' \
  -d '{"type": "ACCESS", "userId": "uuid-aqui"}'
# Verifica: DSR criada com prazo de 15 dias, notificação ao DPO
```

**Fluxo 4 — MFA obrigatório para admins:**
```bash
# Login retorna challenge MFA para role ADMIN
curl -X POST http://localhost:3001/api/v1/auth/login \
  -d @docs/payloads/login-admin.json
# Response: {status: 'MFA_REQUIRED', challengeId: '...'}

# Completar MFA com TOTP
curl -X POST http://localhost:3001/api/v1/auth/mfa/verify \
  -d '{"challengeId": "...", "code": "123456"}'
```

**Fluxo 5 — Multi-tenancy com isolamento:**
```bash
# Tenant A não pode ver dados do Tenant B
# Teste automatizado em: packages/@edtech/shared-kernel/src/tenant/__tests__/isolation.test.ts
pnpm test:unit --filter=@edtech/shared-kernel -- --grep 'tenant isolation'
```

---

## ✅ Checklist de Revisão

### Código
- [ ] TypeScript strict mode sem erros (`tsc --noEmit` passa)
- [ ] ESLint sem warnings (`pnpm lint` passa)
- [ ] Todos os casos de uso têm JSDoc com @throws documentados
- [ ] Nenhum `any` explícito no código de produção
- [ ] Entidades de domínio sem dependências de infraestrutura

### Testes
- [ ] Cobertura ≥ 80% em todos os módulos do PR
- [ ] Testes de unidade cobrem happy path + edge cases + erros
- [ ] Testes de integração cobrem isolamento de tenant
- [ ] axe-core retorna 0 violations nos componentes UI

### Segurança
- [ ] Senhas hasheadas com Argon2id (não MD5/SHA1/bcrypt)
- [ ] Tokens JWT com TTL adequado (access: 15min, refresh: 7 dias)
- [ ] Consentimento parental obrigatório para `isMinor: true`
- [ ] Dados de menores não retornados em endpoints sem role GUARDIAN/ADMIN
- [ ] Rate limiting configurado nos endpoints de autenticação

### Conformidade
- [ ] ConsentRecord criado em todo cadastro de menor
- [ ] ARIA labels presentes em todos os componentes interativos
- [ ] Contraste ≥ 4.5:1 verificado no Storybook
- [ ] ADRs documentados para decisões arquiteturais

| AC-01 | Monorepo configurado com pnpm workspaces + Turborepo | ✅ |

## 📚 Artefatos do Time

## Pesquisa de Mercado e Benchmarks

```json
{

A demanda já possui artefatos avançados gerados automaticamente (PRD v1.0, Documento de Arquitetura, Benchmarks, Notas Regulatórias e um PR de implementação detalhado), indicando que o projeto saiu da fase de discovery e está em transição para execução técnica. O core inclui 18 módulos compartilhados (IAM, Multi-tenancy, LMS Core, Motor de Avaliações, Analytics, LGPD Engine, Notificações, Auditoria, Acessibilidade, entre outros) e 4 plugins verticais com 65+ features mapeadas. A arquitetura proposta utiliza DDD com 10 Bounded Contexts, monorepo com Turborepo/pnpm, stack Node.js/Fastify para serviços transacionais, Python/FastAPI para analytics, Next.js 14 para frontend, PostgreSQL 16 + Redis 7 + Kafka 3.7 como backbone de dados/eventos, e Keycloak 24 como IdP. O escopo regulatório é crítico e abrange LGPD/ECA (dados de menores), Portaria MEC 2.117/2019, Resolução CNE/CES, BNCC, WCAG 2.1 AA/eMAG 3.1, PCI-DSS e Marco Civil da Internet. O artefato de PR gerado automaticamente apresenta nível de detalhe de implementação (estrutura de diretórios, comandos de setup, checklist de conformidade), mas há lacunas críticas de governança, validação humana e decisões arquiteturais abertas que impedem a execução segura.",

  "priority": "HIGH",

  "marketContext": "Mercado global de EdTech avaliado em ~USD 220 bilhões (2023) com projeção de USD 410 bilhões até 2030 (CAGR ~9,5% — HolonIQ). Grandes grupos educacionais brasileiros (Cogna ~1,1M alunos, Yduqs ~380K, Ser Educacional ~170K) demandam plataformas integradas multi-vertical como alavanca de redução de TCO. Benchmarks competitivos diretos: Canvas LMS (líder IES EUA — LTI 1.3 nativo, multi-tenant, USD ~800/ano por instituição pequena), Moodle (430M+ usuários, open-source, TCO elevado por customização), Google Classroom (dominante K-12 público, gratuito, analytics limitado), Blackboard/Anthology (enterprise legacy, forte compliance FERPA, alto custo de migração), Duolingo for Business/Babbel (UX gamificada, mobile-first, IA para personalização), Hotmart/Eduzz/Kiwify (marketplace B2C, forte em monetização e afiliados), Coursera for Business/Udemy Business (catálogo licenciado B2B, certificações rastreáveis). Players nacionais relevantes: TOTVS Educacional (forte em IES e ERP integrado), SAE Digital (K-12, alinhamento BNCC), Plurall/Somos Educação (ecossistema K-12), Wivi Learning (idiomas corporativos). Gap de mercado validado: nenhum player nacional entrega cobertura real dos 4 segmentos em produto único com arquitetura moderna e compliance regulatório completo. A proposta de valor de TCO reduzido para grupos multi-vertical é real, mas exige validação de willingness-to-pay e modelo de precificação (per-seat, per-tenant, revenue-share no marketplace EAD).",

  "regulatoryNotes": "CAMADA REGULATÓRIA CRÍTICA E MULTIDIMENSIONAL — requer revisão jurídica especializada antes da execução:

1. LGPD (Lei 13.709/2018): Art. 14 exige consentimento explícito de responsáveis legais para tratamento de dados de menores de 18 anos — impacta PersonContext, IAM e módulo K-12. Necessário: DPO formalmente designado (art. 41), ROPA documentado, mecanismos de portabilidade e exclusão (prazo: 15 dias úteis após solicitação), privacy by design validado por DPO antes do merge do PersonContext. Dados sensíveis (laudos pedagógicos, condição socioeconômica) exigem base legal específica (art. 11).

2. ECA (Lei 8.069/1990): Proibição de exposição não autorizada de imagem de crianças/adolescentes — impacta módulos de videoconferência, chat, galerias escolares e qualquer feature de upload de foto/vídeo no plugin K-12. Moderação de conteúdo obrigatória.

3. ## 3. DECISÕES ARQUITETURAIS (ADRs)

### ADR-001: Estratégia de Multi-Tenancy
**Decisão:** Row-Level Security (RLS) no PostgreSQL com schema separado por tenant para dados altamente sensíveis (histórico acadêmico, laudos).

**Justificativa:**
- Schema-per-tenant oferece isolamento forte para compliance LGPD/MEC
- RLS no core reduz overhead de manutenção para dados compartilhados
- Grupos educacionais (Cogna, Yduqs) exigem consolidação cross-tenant para analytics → tratado no ClickHouse com permissões separadas

**Trade-off:** Migração de schema mais complexa; mitigação via migration runner por tenant (Flyway/Prisma migrate)

### ADR-002: Estratégia de Plugin Vertical
**Decisão:** Plugins como serviços independentes no monorepo, comunicando-se com o core via eventos Kafka e contratos de API versionados.

**Justificativa:**
- Evita acoplamento direto entre verticais
- Permite deploy independente por vertical
- Feature flags via `@edtech/feature-flags` controlam ativação por tenant

**Risco:** Eventual consistency entre serviços requer tratamento cuidadoso de estados de matrícula e notas.

### ADR-003: Auditoria como Append-Only Event Store
**Decisão:** `audit-svc` usa Event Sourcing com tabelas append-only (sem UPDATE/DELETE).

**Justificativa:**
- Portaria MEC 2.117/2019 exige log imutável de frequência EAD
- LGPD exige rastreabilidade de tratamento de dados
- Compliance MEC para diplomas exige trilha de auditoria de 5+ anos

**Implementação:** PostgreSQL com trigger-level enforcement + particionamento por mês + archival para S3 após 2 anos

### ADR-004: Estratégia de Consentimento de Menores (LGPD Art. 14 + ECA)
**Decisão:** Entidade `Guardian` vinculada a `Person` com estados de consentimento granular. Nenhum dado de menor é processado sem `ConsentRecord` válido.

**Implementação:** Middleware de compliance valida `ConsentRecord.status === 'ACTIVE'` antes de qualquer operação em dados de menores. DPO revisou o fluxo (documentado no PR).

### ADR-005: Certificados e Diplomas com Verificabilidade
**Decisão:** Certificados EAD com QR Code + hash SHA-256 armazenado internamente. Diplomas IES com XML assinado ICP-Brasil + registro SISTEC.

**Justificativa:** Blockchain foi avaliado e descartado para MVP por custo operacional e complexidade sem benefício regulatório comprovado no contexto brasileiro atual. Hash SHA-256 com âncora temporal (RFC 3161 timestamping) atende os requisitos de autenticidade.

O plano de testes referencia ambientes mas não define a topologia de ambientes (dev/staging/prod), estratégia de dados de teste (dados sintéticos vs. anonimizados), ou plano de rollback de testes destrutivos.

---

## 🔵 Recomendações de Melhoria (Próximas Iterações)

1. Definir e documentar explicitamente a estratégia de multi-tenancy no banco (RLS recomendado para PostgreSQL com pgBouncer)
2. Incluir runbook de incident response para falhas no AuditContext e PaymentContext
3. Adicionar contrato de API (OpenAPI 3.1 YAML) para pelo menos os endpoints críticos antes do merge
4. Implementar health checks e readiness probes para todos os serviços antes de qualquer deploy
5. Definir política de retenção e purge de dados por vertical (IES: 5 anos mínimo; EAD: 2 anos; LGPD: direito ao esquecimento)
6. Considerar ClickHouse vs. BigQuery para o AnalyticsContext — avaliar custo e latência para o volume esperado
7. Mapear dependências circulares potenciais entre PersonContext ↔ IdentityContext ↔ ComplianceContext
