items.body:
**Found during a full-codebase audit (2026-08-21), check-only pass — not yet fixed. Confirms a risk CLAUDE.md itself already flags as unverified.**

`eve_trader/sqlite_migration.py:39-67` (`_PER_TENANT_TABLES`) lists 24 tables, and the module docstring claims "Only the ~24 per-tenant tables are migrated ... every table's column names/order are identical between the old SQLite schema and the new Postgres one." The actual current schema has **37** RLS-enabled per-tenant tables (25 in `phase1_schema.sql` + 2 in `phase2_schema.sql` + 10 in `doctrine_schema.sql`) — 13 more than the list covers.

**Caveat (so this isn't overstated):** 2 of the missing ones (`tenant_settings`/`tenant_tokens`) correctly have no ETL equivalent since the pre-migration app used `config.yaml`/`tokens.json` instead, and the 10 `doctrine_*` tables are a Postgres-native feature that never existed in the pre-migration SQLite schema — so today's script is not actually lossy for any real pre-migration `.db` file. That said, this is exactly the "newly-added RLS-enabled table that never got added to the migration list" scenario CLAUDE.md's own "Deferred, not rejected" section predicts as the risk of having no drift-guard test for this file — now confirmed to have already happened, not just theoretical.

**Fix direction** (not implemented, report-only): either update `_PER_TENANT_TABLES`'s docstring to be explicit about which categories of table are deliberately excluded (and why), or add the drift-guard test CLAUDE.md describes (live Postgres introspection against `information_schema`/`pg_policies`) — CLAUDE.md itself notes this only matters again for a hypothetical future disaster-recovery migration from an old SQLite backup, so low urgency, but worth tracking.

Severity: **medium** (currently non-lossy in practice, but the underlying drift-detection gap is real and could bite on a future addition).

items.title: Decision: is Airbyte still on the roadmap? (ELT/ETL leaves scope under the multi-tenant direction)
items.body:
## Context

The local Airbyte setup uses `abctl`, which provisions Airbyte into a throwaway kind (k8s-in-docker) cluster on its own Docker network. This is a dev/POC convenience, not a production deployment. Several pain points encountered locally are artifacts of `abctl`, not the design:

- The Airbyte kind node must be manually bridged to the `open_epm` Docker network (`docker network connect open_epm airbyte-abctl-control-plane`), and **this bridge drops on every host reboot / Airbyte reinstall** — konsol then can't reach the Airbyte API (all calls fail until re-attached). Documented in `scripts/setup-airbyte.sh` but fragile.
- Airbyte API credentials are random per-install (`abctl local credentials`) and currently hand-pasted into konsol EPM Settings.
- `workspace_id` and `d365_source_definition_id` are found manually via the UI/API.

## What production should look like

Two viable shapes:

**A. Airbyte Cloud (managed SaaS)** — stable API (`api.airbyte.com`), OAuth application client-id/secret created once, stable workspace/source-definition IDs. The ClickHouse **destination** must be reachable from Airbyte Cloud (TLS public endpoint + IP allowlist, or tunnel/PrivateLink). D365 source side is already public HTTPS (Azure OData).

**B. Self-hosted Airbyte on Kubernetes (Helm)** — Airbyte + ClickHouse in the same cluster/VPC, **stable service DNS** (no docker bridge, no reboot-drop). Custom D365 connector image published to a registry (GHCR/ECR), versioned.

## What changes local → prod

| Concern | Local (abctl) | Production |
|---|---|---|
| Networking | manual `docker network connect`, drops on reboot | VPC/cluster service DNS (self-host) or secured endpoint/tunnel (Cloud) |
| Airbyte creds | random per-install, hand-pasted | secret manager (Vault / AWS Secrets Manager / K8s secrets), injected |
| workspace/source-def IDs | hunt in UI/API | set once via IaC (Terraform / Helm values / bootstrap) |
| EPM Settings Airbyte block | clicked in UI | provisioned by config/IaC at deploy time |
| D365 connector | local docker image | published, versioned registry image |
| Stability | reboot breaks it | restart policies, persistence, monitoring, HA |

## What stays the same

The konsol layer is prod-ready as-is: `provision_connector_airbyte` is idempotent (find-or-create), D365 creds stored encrypted in connector password fields, and the config → source → schema-apply → build flow is identical. Productionizing means swapping the Airbyte substrate, not rebuilding konsol.

## Multi-tenant (hosted-clients) notes

- One Airbyte workspace per client (or dedicated instance for isolation); connector → `workspace_id` scopes it.
- Per-tenant D365 creds stay encrypted in each tenant's konsol (never exposed to an LLM/MCP — only a `configured: true` boolean is ever returned).
- Per-tenant ClickHouse target (separate database/schema, e.g. `epm_raw_<tenant>`).
- Onboarding = IaC creating a workspace + connection + calling idempotent `provision_connector_airbyte`, not a human clicking buttons.

## Key decision

The single biggest real design decision is **how Airbyte reaches ClickHouse securely**: in-VPC service DNS (self-host) vs secured endpoint/tunnel (Cloud). Everything konsol-side carries over unchanged.

## Acceptance / next steps

- [ ] Decide Cloud vs self-hosted Helm
- [ ] Define ClickHouse-destination networking for the chosen path
- [ ] Move Airbyte + per-tenant secrets into a secret manager
- [ ] Provision EPM Settings Airbyte block + workspace/source-definition via IaC
- [ ] Publish the `source-d365-fno` custom connector image to a registry

---
_Filed from a working session analyzing the D365 → consolidation wiring on the local stack._

items.title: Epic: Per-tenant email sending domain (donor relances) — verified DKIM/DMARC alignment

labels.name: non-trivial
labels.description: Major version bump or change requiring explicit human review and migration plan — do not auto-merge

labels.name: epic
labels.description: Large body of work that can be broken down into a number of smaller tasks

items.body:
## 0. Why this exists — at a glance

Today every email Givernance sends — donation receipts, team invites, **and donor relances** — leaves from a **single shared `From:` address** resolved by [`resolveEmailFrom()`](https://github.com/purposestack/givernance/blob/main/packages/worker/src/env.ts) (one tenant-agnostic `EMAIL_FROM` env var, fallback `Givernance <no-reply@givernance.local>`). The HTML footer is hardcoded `Sent via Givernance.`

When an NPO operator clicks **Send relance** on a donor multi-select (feature shipped in Epic #274, see `packages/worker/src/processors/send-bulk-email.ts`), the donor receives an appeal **from a domain they don't recognise**. This breaks four things at once:

1. **Donor trust** — recipient never opted in to hear from `givernance.app`, only from their charity. The platform should be invisible.
2. **DMARC alignment** — the org's actual domain isn't on the SPF/DKIM record; the appeal cannot pass strict alignment.
3. **Deliverability under Gmail/Yahoo Feb 2024 bulk-sender rules** — at >5,000 messages/day to either provider, DKIM+SPF+DMARC and RFC 8058 one-click unsubscribe are mandatory, and DMARC alignment requires the From-domain to match the DKIM-signing domain. A shared `givernance.app` From cannot satisfy this. Spam-folder placement jumps from a typical 5–10% baseline to 22–34% for non-compliant senders ([DMARC Report, 2025](https://dmarcreport.com/blog/email-authentication-impact-on-deliverability-spf-dkim-dmarc-inbox-placement)).
4. **Single-bad-tenant reputation contagion** — one rogue tenant on a shared sending pool drops inbox placement 40–60% across the entire customer base ([Mailpool, 2025](https://www.mailpool.ai/blog/multi-tenant-email-architecture-how-agencies-isolate-client-reputation-risk)). For Givernance this is an existential single point of failure.

This work was already aspirationally documented in `docs/05-integration-migration.md` § 3.1 (\"Domain verification: SPF, DKIM, DMARC records per org\") but never implemented. The Epic #274 bulk-email shipment turned a latent doc/code drift into a real product blocker for fundraising.

## 1. Recommendation (MVP)

| Decision | Choice |
|---|---|
| **Sender identity model** | **Subdomain delegation via 3 CNAMEs** (SendGrid \"Automated Security\" pattern). Operator publishes 2 DKIM CNAMEs + 1 Return-Path CNAME on `mail.<their-domain>`. Donor sees `relances@mail.demo-npo.org` with full DMARC alignment. |
| **ESP** | **Resend (EU region)** — already wired (`packages/worker/src/lib/email.ts`), has multi-domain API + EU residency + signable DPA. Suppression scoping (Resend is account-level, not domain-level) handled in our DB to satisfy RGPD Art. 21 per-controller scope. |
| **Transactional vs bulk split** | **Hard split.** Receipts, signup verification, password resets, team invites, MFA codes, security alerts → always platform domain (`givernance.app`). Donor relances + campaign emails → tenant subdomain. Donation tax receipts → tenant subdomain with platform-attestation footer. **Anything authenticating a human or attesting a legal fact stays on `givernance.app`.** |
| **Pricing tier** | **All tiers**, including base. Gating it would be a positioning own-goal vs. our \"transparent, affordable alternative to Salesforce NPSP\" stance. Salesforce gates branded sending behind Marketing Cloud ($10k+/yr) — this is a credible, easily-articulated differentiator. |
| **UX target** | **Mailchimp's verified-domain wizard** — it's the pattern French NPO admins are most likely to have already encountered (Mailchimp is the dominant SMB ESP in France). |
| **Pending-domain policy** | **Hard-block bulk send** when the tenant's domain is configured but unverified (avoid silent fallback to `givernance.app`). Tenants who genuinely have no domain (`@gmail.com`-only NPOs) get a capped fallback on shared `relances.givernance.app` with explicit nudge to acquire a domain (€8–15/yr at OVH/Gandi). |

### Rejected alternatives (with reason)

- **Status quo (single shared `EMAIL_FROM`)** — fails Feb 2024 bulk-sender rules, fails DMARC alignment, exposes platform-wide reputation.
- **Shared domain with per-tenant From-label only** (`\"Demo NPO\" <relances@givernance.app>`) — donor still sees `givernance.app` on hover/expand, DMARC aligned to Givernance only. Useful **only** as the transitional fallback during onboarding, not as the headline solution.
- **Custom apex domain (records on `demo-npo.org` directly)** — Phase 2 upgrade path. SPF 10-lookup limit risk, more onboarding friction; donor-trust gain over subdomain delegation is negligible (donors don't notice `mail.charity.org` vs `charity.org`).
- **Postmark** — no EU region. Reject (EU-only constraint).
- **AWS SES** — operationally heaviest, no first-class multi-tenant identity ergonomics. Phase 3 escape hatch for >100k/month tenants.
- **Brevo (FR-based, originally planned in `docs/05-integration-migration.md` § 3.2 for bulk)** — splitting Resend (transactional) + Brevo (bulk) doubles webhook plumbing, doubles suppression reconciliation, doubles DPA paperwork. Consolidate on Resend until a concrete Brevo-only feature forces the split.
- **Mailgun EU** — feature parity with Resend, switching cost not justified.
- **Scaleway Transactional Email** — does not exist as a first-class product.

## 2. Phasing

### Phase 1 — MVP-blocking (ship before scaling sales beyond design partners)

- New `tenant_email_domains` table (RLS-scoped, one verified domain per tenant initially).
- `EmailSender` interface refactor — add required `tenantId` and `kind: 'transactional' | 'bulk'` parameters. Move From-resolution behind a `SenderIdentityResolver` (cached 60s).
- Resend domain-create + verification poller (worker) with backoff (5 min → hourly, capped at 7 days).
- Settings → **Email sending** UI — Mailchimp-style wizard with 3 copy-paste records + status badge (`pending` → `awaiting_dns` → `verified` / `failed`) + provider-specific screenshots (OVH, Gandi, Cloudflare, Google Domains).
- Free-mailbox deny-list at API layer (`gmail.com`, `yahoo.*`, `outlook.com`, `laposte.net`, `orange.fr`, `free.fr`, etc. — see [Mozilla PSL](https://publicsuffix.org/)).
- `tenant_email_suppressions(org_id, email_hash, suppressed_at, reason)` table — populated from unsubscribe footer + hard-bounce webhooks. **Per-controller scope** (RGPD Art. 21): unsubscribe from Org A does NOT cascade to Org B.
- RFC 8058 one-click List-Unsubscribe header, DKIM-signed, with tenant- and recipient-specific token.
- Operator preview that uses the **real production sending path** (\"send test to me\") — non-negotiable, this is where DMARC misconfigs surface before a real campaign.
- DMARC traffic-light surface (green/amber/red) on the operator dashboard.
- `tenants.physical_address` required field for CAN-SPAM/RGPD footer.
- `docs/24-tenant-email-sending.md` shipping in the same PR (CLAUDE.md doc-discipline rule).
- `diagrams/email-sending-flow.mmd` companion.
- Boot-time guard: hard-fail when `EMAIL_PROVIDER=resend` and `EMAIL_FROM` is unset (currently silently falls back to `Givernance <no-reply@givernance.local>` which is RFC 6761 reserved and gets dropped by receivers — see Risks §5).

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] An org_admin can verify `mail.demo-npo.org` via 3 CNAME records in <30 minutes
- [ ] A bulk relance sent to a Gmail recipient passes DMARC alignment (visible in `Authentication-Results` header)
- [ ] Unsubscribing from Org A does NOT suppress Org B's mailings (per-controller scope verified by integration test)
- [ ] Hard-bouncing a recipient suppresses them only for the originating org
- [ ] Bulk send is hard-blocked with structured 400 (`E_TENANT_DOMAIN_NOT_VERIFIED`) when domain is configured but unverified
- [ ] Transactional path (signup, password reset, team invite) continues to send from `givernance.app` regardless of tenant domain status
- [ ] Tenant offboarding immediately calls `domains.remove` on Resend (DKIM key revoked)
- [ ] Free-mailbox domains rejected at API layer with actionable error message

### Phase 2 — 3–6 months post-MVP

- **Custom apex domain** (Option D) as upgrade path — same UI, SPF-include-flattening warning if existing record nears the 10-lookup limit.
- **Multiple sender domains per tenant** (`dons@`, `evenements@`).
- **Bounce/complaint dashboard** per tenant — complaint rate (Gmail threshold 0.30%), bounce rate, sending volume trend.
- **Per-tenant suppression list management UI** — org_admin add/remove, bulk import during Salesforce ETL migration.
- **DKIM rotation** — manual + scheduled annual.
- **Per-campaign From-name override** (`\"Marie Dupont, Trésorière <relance@asso.org>\"`) — NextAfter data shows +28% open rate from named-human senders ([NextAfter](https://www.nextafter.com/blog/test-different-email-sender-name/)).
- **Federated domain support** — model `domain` as shared org-group resource for federations / dioceses / scout movements where 50 chapters share a parent domain managed by HQ.
- **Weekly re-verification poll** — re-poll DNS post-verification; if records disappear or DKIM selector changes, transition to `reverification_failed`, alert org_admin, gate sends to fallback after 72h.
- **DMARC enforcement nudge** — advisory + suggested DNS record when tenant's apex DMARC is `p=none`.

### Phase 3 — later

- **Dedicated IPs** for >100k/month tenants (likely SES backend, dual-ESP routing by tenant tier).
- **BIMI logo verification** (requires VMC, real money).
- **ARC sealing** for forwarded mail.
- **Automatic SPF flattening** for tenants whose record exceeds the lookup limit.

## 3. Architecture sketch

```
tenant_email_domains
  id              uuid pk
  org_id          uuid fk tenants(id) RLS
  domain          citext not null              -- mail.demo-npo.org
  esp_domain_id   text not null                -- Resend domain id
  status          enum('pending','awaiting_dns','verified',
                       'reverification_failed','revoked')
  verification_records  jsonb                   -- {dkim, spf, returnPath, dmarcSuggestion}
  dkim_selector   text
  verified_at     timestamptz
  last_checked_at timestamptz
  rotation_due_at timestamptz
  created_by      uuid fk users(id)
  created_at, updated_at, deleted_at
  unique(org_id, domain) where deleted_at is null
```

Plus on `tenants`:
- `bulk_sender_domain_id uuid null` (denormalised pointer, one join not a scan)
- `bulk_sender_friendly_name text` (defaults to `tenants.name`, operator override without re-verify)
- `physical_address text not null` (CAN-SPAM/RGPD footer)

Plus `tenant_email_suppressions(org_id, email_hash sha256, suppressed_at, reason enum('unsubscribed','hard_bounce','complaint'))` — per-controller scope, indexed on `(org_id, email_hash)`.

`EmailSender` interface refactor:

```ts
export type EmailKind = 'transactional' | 'bulk';

export interface SendEmailInput {
  tenantId: string;
  kind: EmailKind;
  to: string;
  subject: string;
  html: string;
  text: string;
  replyTo?: string;
}

export interface SenderIdentityResolver {
  resolve(tenantId: string, kind: EmailKind):
    Promise<{ from: string; replyTo?: string; espDomainId?: string; fallbackUsed: boolean }>;
}
```

Pending-domain policy: `kind: 'bulk'` with unverified domain → throw `E_TENANT_DOMAIN_NOT_VERIFIED`. `kind: 'transactional'` → always platform domain, `tenantId` used only for friendly-name and Reply-To.

Full architecture & engagement analysis attached as comments below.

## 4. Open product questions

1. **Shared-fallback policy for tenants without a domain.** Hard-block bulk-send entirely, or cap at first 1000 emails / 30 days on `relances.givernance.app` with friendly From-label? Hard-block is deliverability-safe; soft-cap is onboarding-friendly.
2. **DNS-record ownership in federated structures** (dioceses, scout movements, federations of 50 chapters sharing a parent domain managed by HQ). Model `domain` as tenant-scoped or as shared org-group resource? Affects schema, not just UI.
3. **Per-campaign vs tenant-level From-name.** NextAfter argues for human-named senders (+28% opens). Per-campaign override doubles QA surface — MVP fixes at tenant level, Phase 2 adds per-campaign?
4. **Resend account region.** Is the current Resend account already on EU region, or US? DKIM keys are bound to the account, so a US→EU migration is non-trivial.
5. **DMARC enforcement push.** Recommend (or require) tenant move their *own* domain's DMARC to `p=quarantine` after 30 days of healthy sending? Recommending = good citizenship + improves the tenant's overall security; requiring = hostile because it affects email channels we don't control. Probably an \"advisory with one-click suggested DNS record\" pattern, but it's a positioning call.

## 5. Risks

- **Latent boot failure** — `resolveEmailFrom()` falls back to `Givernance <no-reply@givernance.local>` when `EMAIL_FROM` is unset. `.local` is RFC 6761 reserved (mDNS) and is silently dropped or hard-rejected by Resend. The bulk processor's per-recipient try/catch (`send-bulk-email.ts:107-115`) hides this as `failed` increments in logs. **Audit Loki for the past 30 days before this rolls out**, and add a boot-time guard.
- **Worker RLS context** — `data.orgId` is on the job payload, but the worker has no `app_current_organization_id()` GUC equivalent for ESP calls. When `SenderIdentityResolver` queries `tenant_email_domains`, must use `set_config('app.current_org_id', ...)`. **Open question: does the worker already do this for outbox-driven jobs?** If not, this work expands beyond email — it's a worker-RLS hardening project.
- **Bulk send is sequential** (`send-bulk-email.ts:94`). At 200-tenant scale with 1k recipients per campaign, single-threaded send means ~30-min jobs. Per-tenant domain feature **amplifies volume** (operators send more confidently when delivery looks legit). Consider per-domain rate-limiter + parallelisation before Phase 2.
- **Domain hijack on churn** — tenant offboards, lets `demo-npo.org` lapse, attacker buys it, re-creates CNAME pointing at us. Mitigation: immediate `domains.remove` on offboarding (don't wait for CNAME removal) + 30-day deny-list of recently-removed domains requiring platform_admin approval to re-add.
- **Reputation pool contagion** — Resend default is shared IPs. One bad tenant drags the pool. Mitigations: enforce double-opt-in on imported lists (Phase 2), throttle bulk per-tenant per-hour at BullMQ rate-limit level, earmark Phase 3 dedicated-IP path for >100k/month.

## 6. Documentation deliverables

Per CLAUDE.md doc-discipline rule, this Epic ships with:

- `docs/24-tenant-email-sending.md` — Why this exists, user flow Mermaid, ERD, architecture (incl. transactional/bulk split rationale), readiness gates, suppression-list scope (RGPD Art. 21), permissions matrix, GDPR/CAN-SPAM/CASL posture, future work.
- `diagrams/email-sending-flow.mmd` — End-to-end sequence (operator → DNS verify → send → bounce → suppression).
- Update to `docs/05-integration-migration.md` § 3 (mark as implemented, link to doc 24).
- New ADR in `docs/15-infra-adr.md` — \"ADR-NN: Per-tenant subdomain delegation for bulk email; transactional stays on platform domain.\"

## 7. References

- [Google sender guidelines (Feb 2024)](https://support.google.com/a/answer/81126)
- [RFC 8058 — One-Click List-Unsubscribe](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8058)
- [CNIL Sheet 15 — legal basis for direct marketing](https://www.cnil.fr/en/sheet-ndeg15-take-account-legal-basis-technical-implementation)
- [GDPR Art. 21 — right to object](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-21-gdpr/)
- [M+R Benchmarks 2025 — fundraising email metrics](https://mrbenchmarks.com/charts/email-messaging)
- [SendGrid Automated Security — 3-CNAME pattern](https://support.sendgrid.com/hc/en-us/articles/21415314709147-SendGrid-Automated-Security-Domain-Authentication)
- [Mailchimp — domain authentication wizard](https://mailchimp.com/help/set-up-email-domain-authentication/)
- [Mailpool — multi-tenant reputation contagion](https://www.mailpool.ai/blog/multi-tenant-email-architecture-how-agencies-isolate-client-reputation-risk)
- Code refs: `packages/worker/src/lib/email.ts`, `packages/worker/src/env.ts:resolveEmailFrom`, `packages/worker/src/processors/send-bulk-email.ts`, `packages/api/src/modules/constituents/bulk-email-service.ts`
- Existing aspirational doc: `docs/05-integration-migration.md` § 3.1 + § 3.2

## 8. Companion analyses

- Full **technical architecture analysis** posted as comment below (architect-reviewer agent, ESP comparison, DNS verification flow, suppression-list scope rationale, security/abuse vectors, per-phase acceptance criteria).
- Full **engagement / regulatory / competitive landscape analysis** posted as comment below (research-analyst agent, deliverability impact with citations, M+R benchmarks, Salesforce NPSP / Bloomerang / Mailchimp / EveryAction comparison, NPO onboarding friction reality check, donor-trust UX patterns).

---

**Blocks:** none currently — Epic #274 (postal campaigns) shipped without this gate but the relance feature is **production-ready in code only**; recommend disabling or capping the bulk-email Send button to design partners until Phase 1 of this Epic ships.

Filing gate ①, finding class (b): a named producer prints text to the author that breaks a stated rule, and the gate that owns the rule does not read those positions. Found by the #19123 dev round (PR #20226, `out_of_scope_findings[0]`). Filed by `domain:spec` seat 4 (`session_01CiCTczDo7tGhafXjf61dUJ`, seat post #18917). ⛔ Not graded or routed here; ⛔ not a claim.

## The rule

`AGENTS.md` (`origin/main` `93cfc3f59`, lines 16–18): 「Runtime strings — refusal prose, prescriptions, anything an author is shown — carry no tracker number (`pnpm check:doc-authoring`): the lesson goes into the text.」

## The producer, read by this seat

`packages/cli/src/commands/migrate/meta.ts` (about :519–526 on `93cfc3f59`) prints each semantic TODO to the author:

```
⚠ [protocol N] surface → ${t.replacement}
    why:    ${t.reason}
    verify: ${t.acceptanceCriteria}
```

The three fields come from the ADR-0087 semantic entries under `packages/spec/src/migrations/entries/**`. So their text is 「anything an author is shown」.

## The measurement

- The #19123 dev round, relayed (⛔ this seat did not re-run the REST probe): across `packages/spec/src/migrations/**`, those positions hold **2,060 tracker-id sites (478 distinct numbers)**. **178** of those sites cite numbers that answer **404** today (deleted, not moved: the census found 0 answering 301). PR #20226's body carries the census method and its controls.
- This seat's own corroboration, at `93cfc3f59`: `git grep -c -E '#[0-9]{4,5}\b'` over `packages/spec/src/migrations/entries/**` counts **1,529 lines in 590 files**. That count is line-level and wider than the three positions, so it is an upper bound, not the same instrument.
- `pnpm check:doc-authoring` exits 0 over all of them. Rule 3 does not recognise the `reason` / `replacement` / `acceptanceCriteria` positions, and Rule 3b excludes `packages/spec/src`.

## Why it matters

An operator running `os migrate meta` on a real project reads 「why:」 and 「verify:」 lines that send them to tracker numbers. Some of those numbers no longer exist (178 sites), and the rest can disappear in turn: #19123 measured an 11.7–15.1% one-week decay. The lesson each entry exists to teach is then behind a link instead of in the text the author is reading.

items.body:
## Problem Statement

A founder who wants to try C-thru today must run `docker compose up`, provision their own Postgres, and manage their own server before they can see a single event. This is a real barrier to *evaluating* the product — a founder has to commit to infrastructure before they've seen any value at all. There is no way to try C-thru in the two minutes it takes to paste a script tag; self-hosting is the only path in, and it's a real commitment before any payoff.

## Solution

C-thru v1.0 adds a free, hosted version at cthru.com: a founder signs up, gets a snippet, pastes it into their app, and sees real captured events within about two minutes — no server, no Docker, no database to manage. It is the exact same product underneath (the Spine, the AST guard, the rules engine, session replay masking — every decision D-01 through D-37 stays intact); v1.0 adds a hosting layer on top, it does not change core product behavior. Hosted is explicitly positioned as the trial/evaluation path; self-hosted remains the production/serious-usage path with no caps and full data control. There is no billing, no payment system, and no paid tier in v1.0 — it is free for every hosted founder. Hard, structural per-tenant limits (not policy, not convention) take the place of a billing-based cost control, because there is no revenue to recover cost from.

The single biggest shift underneath this: v0.1–v0.5 is one founder, one copy, their server, their database — the founder is the data controller, and C-thru touches no one's data. v1.0 is multiple founders sharing the operator's infrastructure — the operator becomes a data processor for all of them. This changes the engineering (tenant isolation must be structural, not conventional), the security (a shared-key-store threat model where D-11's env-var approach is no longer adequate), and the legal exposure (a DPA is required before the first signup, not just before session replay ships).

## User Stories

1. As a founder evaluating C-thru, I want to sign up with email/password or Google, so that I can start trying the hosted product without a new, unfamiliar credential system.
2. As a founder, I want to name my project immediately after signup, so that my events have somewhere to land without extra configuration steps.
3. As a founder, I want to see my project's snippet and write key immediately after creating my project, so that I can start capturing events right away.
4. As a founder, I want a live, real-time indicator that flips to "confirmed" the instant my first event arrives, so that I know the snippet is working without navigating away or refreshing.
5. As a founder, I want to see my first auto-captured pageview on the dashboard within about two minutes of pasting the snippet, so that I get real, immediate value before doing any further integration work.
6. As a founder, I want an honest empty state in the Companies section explaining I need to add `identify()` to see company grouping, so that I understand why it's empty rather than assuming it's broken.
7. As a founder, I want a clear "step 2 of 2" indicator for wiring up `identify()`, so that I know exactly what remains before I get full company-grouping value.
8. As a founder, I want a clear "setup complete" state once both the snippet and `identify()` are firing, so that I know I've finished onboarding and am now just using the product.
9. As a founder, I want my hosted data to be completely invisible to every other founder using the same hosted service, so that I can trust shared infrastructure with my own product's data.
10. As the operator, I want tenant isolation enforced by the database itself, not by application code remembering to filter every query, so that a missed `WHERE` clause anywhere in the codebase cannot leak one founder's data to another.
11. As the operator, I want a CI test that fails the build if any table lacks both `relrowsecurity` and `relforcerowsecurity`, so that a newly added table can never silently skip tenant isolation.
12. As the operator, I want every tenant-scoped database access to run inside an explicit transaction with `SET LOCAL app.tenant_id`, so that tenant context can never silently evaporate mid-request due to autocommit behavior.
13. As a founder, I want to bring my own LLM API key (Anthropic, OpenAI, Groq, Gemini, or Grok), so that the hosted product remains free with no usage-based cost to me or the operator.
14. As a founder, I want to be prompted for my LLM key only when I first open `/ask`, not during signup, so that I'm not asked for something before I need it.
15. As a founder, I want per-provider instructions for getting an API key, so that I'm not left guessing where to go for the provider I chose.
16. As a founder, I want my LLM API key stored encrypted, never in plaintext, so that a database breach cannot expose my key.
17. As the operator, I want each founder's LLM key protected by a KMS-managed key rather than an application-level env var, so that decrypting all keys requires compromising a real key-management service, not reading a config file.
18. As the operator, I want a structural test asserting the stored key value never matches the original plaintext key, so that a regression that accidentally stores a key unencrypted is caught immediately, not discovered in a breach.
19. As the operator, I want zero LLM usage cost of my own, so that a popular launch or an abusive actor cannot generate an uncapped bill with no revenue to cover it.
20. As a founder, I want a per-tenant daily event cap, so that another founder's misbehaving integration or a bad actor cannot consume shared infrastructure at my expense.
21. As a founder, I want to see how much of my daily event quota I've used, so that I'm never surprised by a rejected request with no context.
22. As a founder whose events are rejected for exceeding my daily quota, I want a clear error response with a `Retry-After` header telling me when the quota resets, so that I know exactly when ingestion will work again.
23. As the operator, I want the event quota enforced by a durable Postgres counter, not an in-memory counter, so that the limit holds correctly across serverless cold starts where in-memory state doesn't persist.
24. As the operator, I want each tenant's daily cap individually adjustable without a code deploy, so that I can raise or lower limits for debugging, trusted early adopters, or edge cases without shipping new code.
25. As the operator, I want an aggregate ingestion monitor that alerts me as total usage across all tenants approaches a known infrastructure threshold, so that I can make a deliberate decision (pause signups, upgrade plan) before shared infrastructure is actually overwhelmed.
26. As a founder, since session replay is not available at v1.0 launch, I want a clear message explaining it's not yet available on the hosted product, so that I don't think the feature is broken.
27. As the operator, I want the session-replay ingestion endpoint to hard-reject with a clear status rather than silently accept and discard, so that no replay data or replay-related storage cost accrues before the feature is legally cleared.
28. As the operator, I want session replay re-enabled only after a dedicated legal review of the disclosure/consent flow, so that the product never processes real people's screen recordings without that review completed.
29. As the operator (for when replay eventually re-enables), I want a hard per-tenant storage cap — not just a retention window — enforced by a maintained running counter, so that no single founder's session recordings can consume unbounded shared storage.
30. As the operator, I want the per-tenant storage counter reconciled nightly against actual stored bytes, so that counter drift from rolled-back transactions never causes the enforced quota to silently diverge from reality.
31. As the operator, I want a documented aggregate storage threshold that triggers a migration to object storage, so that the single-Postgres architecture has a known, planned-for change point rather than degrading unexpectedly.
32. As a prospective hosted founder, I want a Terms of Service, Privacy Policy, and Data Processing Addendum in place before I can sign up, so that I understand what happens to my data and my end users' data before I commit to using the hosted product.
33. As the operator, I want the Privacy Policy and DPA to accurately describe the real engineered mechanisms (RLS, retention, storage caps, encryption), not generic boilerplate, so the legal documents are never misleading about what actually happens to the data.
34. As the operator, I want the DPA to name the actual subprocessors (hosting, database, and KMS providers) before the product launches publicly, so founders have an accurate record of who touches their data.
35. As a founder currently self-hosting C-thru, I want self-hosted C-thru to continue to exist and be maintained exactly as before, so v1.0's hosted offering doesn't force me to change how I already use the product.
36. As a founder considering switching from self-hosted to hosted, I want an honest answer that there is no automatic data migration path, so I don't assume my historical data will silently appear if I switch.
37. As a founder who does switch to hosted, I want to know that my small configuration (readiness rules, key events, blocked domains, suppression list) can be manually re-entered quickly, so switching doesn't feel more painful than it actually is.
38. As a founder evaluating whether to self-host or use hosted, I want clear, honest positioning that hosted is capped and meant for evaluation while self-hosted has no caps and full data control, so I choose the right option for my needs rather than defaulting to whichever is easier without understanding the trade-off.
39. As the operator, I want hosted infrastructure to run on free tiers during pre-launch development and upgrade to paid tiers exactly at public launch, so costs aren't paid before there's real usage, but also aren't deferred past the point where free-tier limitations (inactivity pausing, non-commercial terms) would cause real problems for real founders.
40. As the operator, I want one project per hosted account in v1.0 (no multi-project support), so the initial build stays minimal and multi-project complexity is only added once real demand justifies it.
41. As a founder, I want the hosted sign-up flow to require no plan selection, no team setup, and no billing information, so the free, no-billing nature of v1.0 is reflected honestly in the actual experience, not just in marketing copy.

## Implementation Decisions

**D-38 — Tenant isolation via Postgres Row-Level Security, not application-layer filtering.**
Every table gets `tenant_id UUID NOT NULL`. Every table has RLS enabled *and forced*: `ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;` — `FORCE` is required, because without it the table-owner role bypasses RLS entirely. Policy shape: `USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid)`. The application's Postgres role must not be the table owner, or RLS grants nothing. A CI test queries `pg_class` (`relnamespace = 'public'::regnamespace AND relkind = 'r'`) and asserts every table (with a small, explicitly named exception list for genuinely global tables) has both `relrowsecurity` and `relforcerowsecurity = true` — failure names the specific offending table.

Tenant context is set via `SET LOCAL app.tenant_id`, which only holds for the current transaction — so every tenant-scoped DB access must run inside an explicit transaction, never autocommit. A single wrapper function is the only door in:

```ts
async function withTenant<T>(tenantId: string, fn: (client: PoolClient) => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  const client = await pool.connect()
  try {
    await client.query('BEGIN')
    await client.query('SET LOCAL app.tenant_id = $1', [tenantId])
    const result = await fn(client)
    await client.query('COMMIT')
    return result
  } catch (e) {
    await client.query('ROLLBACK')
    throw e
  } finally {
    client.release()
  }
}
```

Every module that currently calls the bare connection pool directly (the ingestion path, dashboard queries, the readiness engine, funnels, etc.) is changed to accept a client from `withTenant` instead. This is a real, significant migration across most of the existing data-access layer — not a small patch — even though it changes no product *behavior*.

**D-39 — Session replay storage quota: 1GB / 14-day cap per tenant for hosted (distinct from D-33's self-hosted ceiling, which is unchanged), enforced by a maintained counter, not a `SUM` scan.**
A running counter (e.g. `bytes_used BIGINT` on a tenant storage row) is updated atomically in the same transaction as each chunk insert (`UPDATE ... SET bytes_used = bytes_used + $chunk_size`). The pre-write ingestion check reads the counter; writes past quota are rejected. D-31's existing nightly retention job gains a reconciliation pass (`SET bytes_used = actual SUM(...)`) to correct drift from rolled-back transactions. Aggregate `session_recording_chunks` storage crossing 200GB is the documented trigger to migrate from BYTEA to an S3-compatible object store with path-references (recalibrating D-33's architecture for many-tenants-add-up rather than one-founder's-disk).

**Session replay is hard-disabled at the product level at v1.0 launch** — not just off-by-default per D-37. The ingestion endpoint returns 503 with a clear message; the Settings replay toggle shows "coming soon." This is stronger than D-37's per-founder off-by-default because it's product-level, making it structurally impossible to launch with replay live before the legal review (D-42) clears. Re-enable in a follow-up release once legal clears it.

**D-40 — LLM key storage: envelope encryption via a real KMS, BYOK only, zero centrally-funded LLM usage.**
Each tenant's LLM API key is encrypted with a per-tenant Data Encryption Key (DEK); each DEK is wrapped by a single Key Encryption Key (KEK) that lives in AWS KMS and never leaves it in raw form. The decrypted key exists in application memory only transiently, at the moment of the LLM call — never persisted decrypted, never returned by any API, never logged (same non-negotiables as D-11, now with a real KMS instead of an env var). A structural test asserts the stored key value never matches the original plaintext key (same proof pattern as D-32's masking test). No trial queries, no house key, no centrally-funded LLM calls of any kind — BYOK is the only model, because a centrally-funded model creates an unbounded cost liability with no billing to recover it. If the KMS is unavailable, LLM calls fail for all tenants — this is a correct, documented failure mode, not a bug (degraded `/ask` is better than decrypting keys without KMS protection).

**D-41 — Onboarding flow and one-project-per-account.**
One signup = one tenant = one project for v1.0; no multi-project, no team/workspace switcher. Flow: sign up (NextAuth: email/password + Google OAuth) → name project (one field, no plan selection, no team setup, no billing) → snippet shown immediately with a live, real-time (SSE/WebSocket, not polling) "waiting for your first event" indicator that flips to confirmed the instant the first event arrives → first auto-captured pageview appears on the dashboard (honest ~2 minute claim, since auto-capture needs no integration beyond the script tag) → a distinct, honestly-labeled second step for `identify()` wiring, with the Companies section showing an honest empty state ("No identified users yet — add identify() to your login flow") rather than hiding the section or implying it will fill automatically → a deliberate "setup complete" state once both steps are done, dismissing the onboarding checklist. `/ask` prompts for an LLM key only when the founder first navigates there, with per-provider instructions (Anthropic, OpenAI, Groq, Gemini, Grok).

**D-42 — Legal gate covers the entire public launch, not just session replay.**
The controller→processor relationship begins at the first `identify()` call (the first time a founder's end user's personal data lands in shared hosted Postgres), not at the first session recording. A base Terms of Service, Privacy Policy, and a standard (non-negotiated, self-serve) Data Processing Addendum — incorporated by reference in the ToS, modeled on the Vercel/Supabase/Render pattern — must exist, lawyer-reviewed, before the first public signup. The Privacy Policy and DPA must accurately describe the real engineered mechanisms (D-38 RLS, D-31 retention, D-39 storage caps, D-40 encryption) rather than generic boilerplate. The DPA must name actual subprocessors, which means infrastructure (D-43) must be locked *before* the DPA can be reviewed. The replay-specific disclosure clause template (D-37) is a separate, later gate — only required before replay is re-enabled, not before the base launch.

**D-43 — Infrastructure: Vercel + Supabase + AWS KMS, free tier pre-launch, paid tier at public launch.**
App hosting: Vercel. Managed Postgres: Supabase (chosen over Neon for RLS being Supabase's flagship, best-documented pattern — lower risk of getting D-38's wiring subtly wrong). KMS: AWS KMS specifically, isolated to a single key with minimal IAM — not a broader AWS commitment. Pre-launch/private-beta runs on free tiers (Vercel Hobby, Supabase free, AWS KMS free tier — 10,000 requests/month permanently free); a Vercel cron job pings Supabase to prevent the free tier's inactivity pause during this phase. Upgrade to Vercel Pro + Supabase Pro (~$20-50/month) is triggered exactly at public launch — the same moment D-42's legal gate takes effect — because Vercel Hobby's non-commercial-use restriction and Supabase's inactivity-pause behavior are both incompatible with a live public commercial product. DPA subprocessors: Vercel Inc., Supabase Inc., Amazon Web Services Inc. (KMS only).

**D-44 — Event ingestion quota: 100,000 events/day per tenant, enforced by a durable Postgres counter inside the ingestion path, not the existing in-memory limiter.**
The existing self-hosted rate limiter (`isRateLimited()`, in-memory `Map`) is not adequate for hosted's serverless deployment — a Vercel invocation can be a cold start with fresh memory, so an in-memory counter doesn't actually accumulate state across invocations. The hosted path replaces it with a durable Postgres-backed counter (same pattern as D-39's `bytes_used`), sharing the same interface (`isRateLimited()` returns boolean) but a different implementation selected by environment — self-hosted keeps the in-memory version (works correctly there, single process). Schema:

```
tenant_quotas:
  tenant_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES tenants(id),
  events_today INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  quota_date DATE NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE,
  events_daily_cap INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 100000
```

On each event-ingestion call, inside the same transaction as the insert: if `quota_date < CURRENT_DATE`, reset (`events_today = 0`, `quota_date = CURRENT_DATE`) atomically; if `events_today >= events_daily_cap`, reject with HTTP 429 and a `Retry-After` header (seconds until UTC midnight) before touching the events table; otherwise insert the event and increment `events_today` atomically. `events_daily_cap` is a per-tenant column, adjustable without a code deploy. The cap is visible to the founder ("X / 100,000 events today") in Settings/Dashboard — never a silent wall. Separately, an aggregate monitor (a Vercel cron job) checks total daily ingestion across all tenants against a known fraction of Supabase's plan-level compute capacity and alerts (log/email) if crossed — a manual decision point (pause signups, upgrade plan), not an automatic per-request action.

**D-45 — No migration path from self-hosted to hosted, no self-serve tooling, no concierge option.**
Self-hosted and hosted are structurally different schemas (tenant_id, RLS, KMS-encrypted keys, per-tenant quotas exist only in hosted) — there is no trivial copy path; a real migration would be a full ETL job (remap PKs, stamp `tenant_id` on every row, reconcile schema drift, handle storage-cap mismatches), which is unbudgeted scope contradicting v1.0's minimal-build constraint. Concierge (human-assisted) migration is also explicitly rejected — it requires the same ETL understanding as self-serve tooling, just with a human in the loop, and creates an unbounded support commitment with no tooling behind it.

**D-46 — Positioning: hosted is the trial/evaluation on-ramp; self-hosted is the production/serious-usage path.**
The caps (D-39, D-40, D-41, D-44) are not artificial gating for positioning purposes — they exist for real cost/abuse reasons — but they structurally enforce the positioning too: a founder who outgrows them is naturally pushed toward self-hosting, not just advised to. This must be stated explicitly in hosted's signup flow and docs (e.g. "Hosted is capped and your data lives on shared infrastructure — for production use or full control, self-host: same product, same features, one command"), not left implicit.

## Testing Decisions

A good test here asserts external, observable behavior — does a query issued with no tenant filter at all leak another tenant's rows; does an over-quota event get rejected with the right status and header; does the value actually stored for an LLM key ever equal the plaintext — not internal implementation details of how `withTenant` sequences its `BEGIN`/`SET LOCAL` calls internally.

**Primary seam: `withTenant(tenantId, fn)`.** This is the single highest-leverage seam because every tenant-scoped code path in v1.0 — ingestion, dashboard queries, the readiness engine, funnels, `/ask` — is a caller of it; nothing touches tenant-scoped data any other way. Tests here: a query issued through `withTenant` with tenant A's context cannot see tenant B's rows even when the query itself carries no explicit tenant filter; a rolled-back transaction leaves no partial writes; concurrent requests for different tenants do not cross-contaminate `SET LOCAL` state.

**Second seam: the tenant + quota-aware event-ingestion path (extending the existing `processEvent()` seam from D-03).** Tests here: an event under quota is accepted and the counter increments; an event at exactly the cap is accepted and the next one is rejected; a rejected event returns 429 with a `Retry-After` header reflecting seconds to UTC midnight; the quota resets correctly across a UTC-day boundary; per-tenant caps set via `events_daily_cap` are respected individually.

**Two structural/contract tests**, in the same family as the existing `actLoopContracts.test.ts` (D-26's grep test) and D-32's masking proof — verifying a property of the whole system, not one function's behavior through a call site:
- An RLS contract test querying `pg_class` (`relnamespace = 'public'::regnamespace AND relkind = 'r'`), asserting every table (except a small, explicitly named, justified exception list) has both `relrowsecurity` and `relforcerowsecurity = true`.
- An LLM-key-encryption contract test asserting the value actually persisted for a tenant's LLM key never equals the original plaintext key string.

Onboarding's live-confirmation behavior (D-41) is integration/E2E territory, not a unit seam, given it involves an SSE/WebSocket connection and real event arrival — worth a lighter-weight integration test rather than forcing it through the two primary seams above.

## Out of Scope

- Billing, payments, Stripe integration, or any paid tier — explicitly and entirely out of scope for v1.0. Deferred to a future version once real usage and demand are validated.
- Multi-project or multi-workspace support per account.
- Any data migration tooling from self-hosted to hosted, self-serve or concierge/human-assisted.
- Session replay actually being live/usable at v1.0 launch — it is built (D-39's quota mechanism) but hard-disabled at the product level until the dedicated legal review clears it.
- Any centrally-funded or trial LLM usage (no house key, no free query allowance).
- Redis, Upstash, or any external rate-limiting service — the hosted quota mechanisms (event and storage) live entirely in Postgres.
- A negotiated, per-customer DPA process — only a standard, self-serve DPA incorporated by reference in the ToS.
- IP-based geographic blocking or any consent-enforcement mechanism beyond what D-37 already established.
- Any change to self-hosted C-thru's behavior, or to any of D-01 through D-37.

## Further Notes

- Sequencing dependency: D-43 (infrastructure) must be locked before D-42's DPA can be lawyer-reviewed, since the DPA names specific subprocessors by name. The order is infrastructure → DPA drafted against real subprocessors → lawyer review of all three legal documents → public launch. Not: launch first, update the DPA when infrastructure changes later.
- The numbers set here (100,000 events/day, 1GB/14-day replay cap, 200GB aggregate migration trigger, ~$20-50/month infra estimate) are v1.0 starting points, deliberately made adjustable without a schema change (e.g. the per-tenant `events_daily_cap` column) — not intended to be permanent or precisely optimal on day one.
- Open implementation note for whoever picks this up: D-39's storage-quota mechanism (counter, reconciliation, aggregate-threshold monitoring) should likely be built now even though the replay ingestion endpoint stays hard-disabled (503) at launch — so that re-enabling replay later is a matter of removing a feature flag, not a new build. This wasn't pinned down as a hard requirement during design and is a reasonable judgment call for implementation.
- This PRD assumes the existing self-hosted data-access layer (most modules currently calling the bare `db` pool directly) will need a mechanical signature change to accept a client from `withTenant` instead. This is real, nontrivial migration scope across most of `src/lib/*.ts` — flagged explicitly so it isn't discovered mid-implementation as a surprise.

items.title: Test wall: backend integration suite (harness + API journeys)
items.body:
## Decision Summary

- Runner: pytest + pytest-django (Django-3.1-compatible 4.5.x-era pin), single runner for both suites; existing ~151 `APITestCase` unit tests run unchanged, no rewrite
- Parallelism: pytest-xdist; each worker gets its own test database (with tenant universe) and its own Redis logical DB
- Tenant universe: fixed session-scoped cast — `org-a`, `org-b`, plus the personal/public workspace — built once per run per worker via `django_db_setup`
- Per-test isolation: transaction rollback (django-tenants switches schemas via `search_path` on one connection, so one rollback covers all schemas); commit-requiring tests (websocket) marked `slow_lane` (truncate-based)
- Redis: real service (no fakeredis); worker *n* → Redis DB *n* via cache and channels `LOCATION` override; `flushdb` per test; the existing unit suite's `flushall` teardown gets the same fix
- Test data: factory_boy factories per model (SubFactory graphs; traits for published/draft and per question type) + thin schema-aware journey builders (e.g. `in_workspace(org_a)`) that own `schema_context()` internally; no fixture files; specs never call `connection.set_schema()`
- Auth mocking: outbound-HTTP boundary only — Google token/userinfo endpoints stubbed with `responses` (convert-token exercises the full internal pipeline); OTP's SNS publish stubbed with botocore stubber (OTP read in-process from DB); SSO unmocked (`AllowAny` endpoint, factories seed the org's `api_key`); all other journeys use a fast `authed_client` fixture minting oauth2_provider tokens directly
- Image upload: file storage overridden to a local backend in test settings (same mock-at-the-outbound-boundary principle — the lane must not need AWS credentials); assert the Image record and returned reference
- Layout: `tests/integration/` at repo top level, organized by inventory axis — `auth/`, `creator/`, `learner/`, `org/`, `misc/`; markers `integration` and `slow_lane`; `pytest -m integration` runs the lane alone
- Style: plain pytest, no BDD layer; actor fixtures (`creator`, `learner` as pre-authed clients); permission matrix parametrized within `org/`
- Runtime budget: lane ≤5 min CI wall-clock (xdist, stock runner); whole backend test job ≤ ~10 min; everything blocks PRs by default, `slow_lane`/nightly demotion only on demonstrated, profiled budget pressure
- Coverage wiring rides with this workstream: committed `.coveragerc` (source scoped to app packages; omit migrations/tests/settings/wsgi/asgi; branch coverage on); unit and integration as separate CI lanes → separate Codecov flags (v5 action, `CODECOV_TOKEN`, `fail_ci_if_error: true`) → separate committed floors enforced by CI itself; floors initialize at first measured −1%; job summary prints "measured X% vs floor Y%" and nudges when the gap exceeds ~2%
- Sequencing: harness slice merges first and unblocks the four unit-fill issues (#375–#378)
- New dev dependencies only: `pytest`, `pytest-django` (3.1-compatible pin), `pytest-xdist`, `factory_boy`, `responses` — nothing enters production requirements

## Problem Statement

Main runs Django 3.1.1 with an unmerged upgrade chain to 5.2 LTS waiting behind it. The existing ~151 unit tests cover isolated CRUD per app but no real user journeys: nothing exercises the tenant middleware end to end, none of the three auth flows beyond OTP/SSO basics, no websocket path, and the permission matrix (member/non-member/superuser × workspace × visibility) is untested. The reported 97.66% coverage is inflated — no coverage configuration exists, so the number measures the wrong universe without branch coverage. Merging the Django chain against this wall is not safe: upgrade risk concentrates exactly where journey coverage is absent (ORM/tenancy, middleware/auth, caching).

## Solution

Build the backend integration test lane: API-journey tests that exercise the real Django app, tenant Postgres, and Redis — no browser — covering the journey inventory (#363) in depth. A developer runs the whole lane locally with one documented command against the standard docker-compose stack; CI runs it as its own lane with its own Codecov flag and committed coverage floor. The harness slice (runner wiring, factories, builders, tenant/Redis fixtures, skeleton, CI lane split) merges first so the per-app unit-fill workstreams can proceed in parallel with journey-writing. Once green, the per-PR validation runbook (#370) runs this lane on every Django-chain PR.

## User Stories

1. As a maintainer merging the Django upgrade chain, I want API-journey tests over the real app, tenant Postgres, and Redis, so that each chain PR is validated where upgrade risk actually concentrates.
2. As a backend developer, I want to run the entire integration lane with one documented command against my docker-compose stack, so that I can verify changes locally before pushing.
3. As a backend developer, I want the existing ~151 unit tests to run unchanged under pytest, so that the runner switch costs nothing and there is one way to run tests.
4. As a unit-fill contributor (#375–#378), I want shared factories and journey builders from the harness slice, so that I can write per-app tests without inventing my own data setup.
5. As a test author, I want schema-aware builders like `in_workspace(org_a)`, so that I never manipulate `connection.set_schema()` by hand and cannot leak tenant state between tests.
6. As a test author, I want actor fixtures (`creator`, `learner`) that arrive pre-authenticated, so that journey specs read as user behavior rather than auth ceremony.
7. As a maintainer, I want all three auth flows tested with only their external legs mocked, so that the internal auth stack the Django chain touches (social-auth → drf-social-oauth2 → user creation → token issuance) is genuinely exercised.
8. As an organization admin, I want the full permission matrix (member / non-member / superuser × personal / org workspace × public / private plio) enforced by parametrized tests, so that tenancy and access regressions cannot merge silently.
9. As a creator, I want publish rules, duplicate/copy-to-workspace, metrics, CSV report contents, and soft-delete semantics covered by journey tests, so that my authoring workflows survive the upgrade.
10. As a learner, I want session lifecycle, answer persistence per question type, the event stream, watch-time computation, and scorecard math covered, so that playback and progress behavior stays correct.
11. As a reviewer, I want the integration lane to finish within 5 minutes of CI wall-clock (whole backend job ≤ ~10 min), so that it blocks PRs without slowing iteration.
12. As a maintainer, I want unit and integration coverage reported as separate Codecov flags with committed floors that CI itself enforces, so that coverage is truthful per lane and can only ratchet upward.
13. As a maintainer, I want every CI run to print measured coverage versus the floor, so that drift is visible before it becomes a fight.
14. As a developer running tests in parallel, I want per-worker databases and per-worker Redis logical DBs with `flushdb` (never `flushall`), so that xdist workers cannot corrupt each other's state.
15. As a maintainer, I want the websocket live-users happy path tested through channels, so that the channels version bump in the chain has a canary.
16. As a future debugger, I want the `tests/integration/` file tree organized by journey axis, so that the tree itself doubles as the coverage checklist against the inventory.

## Implementation Decisions

### Runner and configuration
- pytest + pytest-django, pinned to a release compatible with Django 3.1 (4.5.x era). The pin is bumped mid-chain at the Django 5.0 step — that bump is a runbook line item in #370, not this workstream's job. Pins must also work on Python 3.8 (the CI/Dockerfile interpreter).
- One runner for both suites. The existing per-app `tests.py` modules run unchanged under pytest's Django test-case collection. Lane selection: the integration lane is `pytest -m integration`; the unit lane is everything outside `tests/integration/`.
- A dedicated test-settings layer (settings module or conftest-level overrides) handles: per-worker Redis logical DB for both the cache and the channels layer, local file-storage override, `SMS_DRIVER` unset so the SNS path is never live by accident.

### Tenant universe and isolation
- `django_db_setup` builds the fixed cast once per run per xdist worker: `org-a`, `org-b` (each an Organization whose creation provisions its schema), plus the personal/public workspace (the schema requests land in with no `Organization` header). Role rows already arrive via the users app's data migration; the oauth2 Application (the one named by `API_APPLICATION_NAME`) is seeded once at universe build.
- Per-test isolation is transaction rollback. django-tenants switches schemas by changing `search_path` on the single test connection, so one rollback undoes writes across all schemas touched by a test.
- Tests that require real commits (the channels/websocket journey) are marked `slow_lane` and use truncation-based cleanup. `slow_lane` never dictates the design of the main suite.

### Redis
- Real Redis — already free in CI service containers and local docker-compose; fakeredis adds divergence risk for zero savings.
- Worker *n* maps to Redis logical DB *n* via the cache `LOCATION` override; the channels layer gets the same per-worker override.
- Per-test cleanup is `flushdb` on the worker's own DB. The existing unit suite's `tearDown` currently calls `flushall` (instance-wide — it would wipe other workers' state); that call is replaced with the same `flushdb` approach as part of the harness slice.

### Test data
- factory_boy factories per model: SubFactory graphs across the Plio → Video / Item → Question chain and the entries chain (Session → SessionAnswer / Event); traits for published vs draft and for each question type (mcq, checkbox, subjective).
- Thin journey builders own tenancy: `in_workspace(org_a)` wraps `schema_context()` internally. Specs never call `connection.set_schema()` — a hard rule, enforced in review and by acceptance criteria.
- Fixture files rejected (they rot at every chain migration); ad-hoc ORM setup rejected (duplication already visible in the current suite). These factories are shared vocabulary with the unit-fill issues.

### Auth: two planes
- Mocked plane — external legs only, at the outbound-HTTP boundary:
  - Google convert-token: stub Google's token/userinfo endpoints with `responses`, so the exchange exercises the entire internal pipeline (social-auth backend → drf-social-oauth2 → user creation → internal token issuance) — exactly the stack the Django chain bumps. No custom social pipeline exists today; the default one is what gets tested.
  - OTP over SMS: stub the SNS client at the botocore level; read the generated OTP in-process from the database; assert token issuance and user creation, plus expiry and re-request behavior.
  - SSO: no mocks. It is a plain `AllowAny` endpoint; factories seed the org's `api_key`, and tests assert the minted user is scoped to that org (`auth_org` + `unique_id`).
- Fast plane — every other journey authenticates through an `authed_client` fixture that mints oauth2_provider access tokens directly (same approach the existing suite uses), skipping login journeys entirely.

### Layout and style
- `tests/integration/` at repo top level: `auth/`, `creator/`, `learner/`, `org/`, `misc/` mirroring the journey inventory axes. The tree is the coverage checklist.
- Markers: `integration` on the whole lane, `slow_lane` on commit-requiring tests.
- Plain pytest, no BDD layer. Readability comes from builders and actor fixtures. The tenancy/permission matrix is parametrized within `org/`.

### CI restructure and coverage wiring
- The single test job splits into unit and integration lanes (same service containers: Postgres + Redis).
- Committed `.coveragerc`: `source` scoped to the app packages; omit migrations, tests, settings, wsgi/asgi; branch coverage on.
- Each lane uploads to Codecov under its own flag — Codecov revived strictly as visibility: v5 action, `CODECOV_TOKEN` (already provisioned, #373), `fail_ci_if_error: true`. This replaces the current tokenless v1 action.
- Enforcement lives in CI, not Codecov: a committed floor file per lane; the job fails under the floor. Floors initialize at first measured value −1%. Every run prints "measured X% vs floor Y%" in the job summary and nudges when the gap exceeds ~2%.
- The honest consequence is accepted: today's 97.66% is inflated (no coverage config exists); the scoped, branch-on number will be lower and becomes the truthful baseline.

### Sequencing: harness slice first
The first merged slice contains: pytest/pytest-django/xdist wiring, factories + builders, tenant-universe and Redis fixtures, the `tests/integration/` skeleton with one smoke journey, and the CI lane split with coverage wiring. Merging it unblocks the four unit-fill issues (#375–#378), which then proceed in parallel with journey-writing.

### Coverage target (what the lane must test)
The integration section of the journey inventory (#363), happy path + edge cases, weighted toward Django-upgrade risk (ORM/tenancy, middleware/auth, caching):

- **Auth:** Google convert-token; OTP over SMS (request, verify, expiry); third-party SSO with per-org `api_key` scoping.
- **Creator:** full CRUD on plios/items/questions; publish rules (publish with no questions, edit-after-publish); invalid video URL; duplicate and copy-to-workspace (tenant correctness); metrics correctness; CSV report contents including watch-time rounding; soft-delete semantics; settings persistence; image upload.
- **Learner:** session lifecycle including retries and carry-over from the previous session; answer persistence per question type; event stream (played/paused/skipped); watch-time computation; skip-enabled rules; scorecard math; experiments A/B splitting; public vs private access rules.
- **Org/tenancy — exhaustive:** the full permission matrix (member / non-member / superuser × personal / org workspace × public / private plio) as parametrized tests; tenant isolation across every entity type; org membership lifecycle; SSO `api_key` scoping per org.
- **Misc:** websocket live-user updates via the channels test communicator (happy path — also the canary for the channels bump); Django admin smoke.

## Testing Decisions

- **Seams (two, both existing; no new seams):**
  1. **The HTTP API surface** — DRF's test client driving real requests through the full middleware stack, with the `Organization` header selecting the tenant schema exactly as production does. This is the highest existing seam and carries every journey except one. Assertions observe responses and, where state matters, subsequent API reads — not internal queries.
  2. **The ASGI websocket boundary** — channels' test communicator against the user consumer route, for the live-users journey only. An existing public boundary, not a new seam.
- **What makes a good test here:** specs assert external behavior (status, response shape, cross-tenant visibility, tokens issued), never implementation details (no reaching into cache key formats or `search_path` internals). Builders replacing manual schema switching is itself a seam-hygiene rule: the header is the tenancy interface under test.
- **Independent source of truth for expected values:** scorecard math, watch-time (including CSV rounding), and metrics expectations are hand-computed from deliberately constructed event/answer timelines and stated as literals in the tests — never derived by re-running the application's own query builders or aggregation code. CSV assertions check actual cell values of the constructed scenario, not just file presence (the current suite only asserts a `FileResponse` comes back).
- **Modules under test:** users (all three auth flows and the consumer), plio (creator journeys, cache-touching reads, reports), entries (learner journeys), organizations (tenancy middleware and the permission matrix).
- **Prior art:** the existing suite's `BaseTestCase(APITestCase)` pattern — bearer-token credentials plus the `Organization` header — is the stylistic ancestor of `authed_client`; the lane keeps that request idiom while replacing its manual `connection.set_schema()` calls and `flushall` teardown with builders and per-worker `flushdb`.

## Out of Scope

- Browser journeys — the e2e workstream (#380); anything frontend (#379).
- Product changes to make features testable; fixing pre-existing main bugs the suite exposes (file new issues; keep this workstream lean).
- Load testing.
- Tests for the `experiments` and `tags` apps — abandoned in production, conscious skip (#366). (The learner-side A/B splitting journey stays in scope; the apps' own CRUD does not.)
- The `etl` app's endpoints — not in the journey inventory; unit coverage arrives via its unit-fill issue.
- Bumping the pytest-django pin for Django 5.0 — a #370 runbook line item mid-chain, not this workstream.
- Replacing the deprecated Python 3.8 CI/Docker interpreter — separate concern; all new pins must simply remain 3.8-compatible.

## Further Notes

**Known risks (carried from #367):**
- The pytest/pytest-django pins must survive Django 3.1→5.2; the mid-chain bump at the 5.0 step may need harness adjustments — an explicit chain step, not a surprise.
- xdist × session fixtures: each worker builds its own database and tenant universe; verify boot cost stays acceptable at the chosen worker count.
- Rollback isolation assumes single-connection `search_path` switching holds across django-tenants bumps; if it breaks, isolation degrades to truncate and the budget needs revisiting.
- channels era-gap: the happy-path websocket test doubles as the canary for the channels version bump.

**Discovered context that shapes the work:**
- The current CI job installs only production requirements; the new dev dependencies mean CI must install the dev requirements file (or a dedicated test-requirements file) in the test lanes.
- Role rows are seeded by a data migration and the oauth2 Application by a management command at boot — the tenant-universe fixture must guarantee both exist per worker database rather than assuming them.
- Default file storage is S3 with real credentials in CI today; the storage override removes that external dependency from the test lanes.
- With no `Organization` header and `DEFAULT_TENANT_SHORTCODE` unset, requests land in the public schema — the "personal workspace" member of the tenant universe must reflect the environment's actual default-tenant configuration.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] `pytest -m integration` runs the whole lane locally with one documented command against the dev's docker-compose stack (binding local-first criterion from map #362)
- [ ] Every axis of the coverage target has specs; the tenancy/permission matrix is parametrized and exhaustive
- [ ] The existing ~151 unit tests pass unchanged under pytest
- [ ] Integration lane ≤5 min CI wall-clock; whole backend test job ≤ ~10 min
- [ ] No spec calls `connection.set_schema()` directly; no `flushall` remains anywhere in the test suite
- [ ] `.coveragerc` scoped with branch coverage on; unit and integration upload as separate Codecov flags (v5, `fail_ci_if_error: true`); committed floor file enforced by CI; both floors initialized at first measured −1%; job summary prints measured-vs-floor
- [ ] Harness slice is the first merged slice and is independently usable by the unit-fill issues (#375–#378)
- [ ] Local run instructions documented in the repo

labels.description: V0 contract item that other V0 work depends on

items.body:
## Why now

The 2026-08-24 end-to-end test (PR #80 build → Jamf Cloud → outbox → HEC → `index=main`) proved the transport and exposed the gap: the delivery-time shaping designed in docs/splunk-event-shaping.md is unbuilt. What lands in Splunk today is the raw canonical delta wrapped in `{"event": ...}` — nested arrays, `spath`/`mvexpand` hostile, indexed at delivery time instead of the event's own time. The event shape is the product's contract and freezes the moment customer SPL is written against it, so the shape itself is the v0 blocker; enrichment payloads are additive later precisely because the shape reserves their keys.

## Rulings (Kyle, 2026-08-24 design session)

1. **Snapshot stream, per app.** Every device sync emits one HEC event per installed application, `sourcetype=jamf:mac:app`. The application object is what Jamf provided, 100% untouched.
2. **Casing law.** Jamf-sourced fields keep Jamf's casing exactly; LoonInspect-minted fields are `snake_case` (`inventory_id`, `short_date`). Fidelity to the source is the naming convention.
3. **`device_meta` as its own key.** Pre-generated once per device sync, duplicated onto every sub-event. Example fields (list not final): `inventory_id`, `hostname`, `serialNumber`, `assignedUser`. The configurable-with-hard-size-cap requirement from the shaping doc stands.
4. **`inventory_id` is the bridge.** A UUID4 minted **per device per sync pass** at the ingest choke point, stamped on every sub-event of that pull across all sourcetypes — `index=x inventory_id=<uuid>` reconstructs the device; dashboards jump Groups ↔ Apps on one token. `jobId` nests above it (one run → many inventory_ids). Delivery retries reuse the same id.
5. **Reserved enrichment keys, current state only.** `patching{}` and `vulnerabilities{}` on the app event carry what IS true about that build. (`alerts{}` is parked — undefined keys don't ship.)
6. **Changes are their own sourcetypes, not inline.** Inline keys describe what IS; sourcetypes describe what HAPPENED. Change events fan out as `jamf:mac:app:change` (and siblings per entity), carrying the policy's `level` as a first-class field for saved-search alerting, `_time` at the observation window, and the new observation's `inventory_id`.
7. **Sourcetype tree is the routing dimension.** `jamf:mac:app` extends to `jamf:mac:app:vuln`, `jamf:mac:app:change`; device anchor and group-membership streams follow the same pattern.
8. **Envelope.** `time` (epoch, from the event's own timestamp per app.core.runs.event_time — never index time), `host` = device hostname, `sourcetype` per event.

Reference shape:

```json
{
  "event": {
    "application": { "...Jamf's app record, untouched..." : "..." },
    "patching": {},
    "vulnerabilities": {},
    "device_meta": {
      "inventory_id": "<uuid4-per-device-per-sync>",
      "hostname": "...",
      "serialNumber": "...",
      "assignedUser": "..."
    }
  },
  "sourcetype": "jamf:mac:app",
  "time": 1756049903
}
```

## v0 blockers — the shape, nothing else

- [ ] A canonical **per-device snapshot event** enqueued each sync (the delta event survives for generic webhooks and change derivation) — the shaping doc's "expand the delta" conclusion cannot produce a snapshot stream and is superseded on this point.
- [ ] **HEC expansion** in/adjacent to `_build_body()`: snapshot event → N per-app events + device anchor, `device_meta` + `inventory_id` stamped on each. Splunk-destination-scoped; other destination types keep the canonical event.
- [ ] **Envelope `time` + `host`** on every HEC event (subsumes the standalone \_time finding from the e2e).
- [ ] **Changes as `:change` sourcetypes** with `level`, window `_time`, `inventory_id`.
- [ ] **Naming conformance pass** against the casing law (today's wire event mixes camelCase meta with snake_case top level).

## Open rulings blocking the above (Kyle)

- **Which Jamf is "what Jamf provides"** — v4's camelCase as sent today, or the Classic-era names migrating add-on SPL was written against. Freezes with the first customer search.
- **Where the raw app record rides** — fattened snapshot payload at enqueue time (cache-don't-calculate) vs. delivery-time join to the observation ledger.
- Final `device_meta` field list (incl. where `short_date` and `jobId` live); empty `{}` vs omitted keys for disabled features.

## Explicitly not v0

- `vulnerabilities{}` population — blocked on the LoonVD/api.loonsec.io lookup feed; the Wireshark fixture work designs the shape and the Global-API wire contract in parallel.
- `patching{}` population — data already exists per app row (#65/#67); additive fast-follow.
- HEC request batching; configurable `device_meta` surface (size cap noted above).

Implementation splits into focused per-session issues off this one; this issue is the contract record and tracking list.

items.title: Phase out orpc backend
items.body:
Whether we want to stay with Go or migrate to another framework, we're 100% going to dump the node env. The reason being that the ORPC+React setup feels very cluttering and awkward to work with.

Either we ship a single go binary or we use something like Phoenix/RoR to handle most of the stuff we need. This includes stuff like handling multi-tenacy stuff.

Opting for Phoenix because:
- Ecto is genuinely good at multi-tenancy and schema flexibility
- LiveView makes building admin panels and dynamic UIs easier without heavy frontend rewrites
- OTP/processes are great for running isolated ETL jobs per tenant
- Database partitioning is well-trodden (prefix-based schemas, separate databases, whatever)

I've already used Phoenix for another project and it seems to suffice our needs.

items.title: INSPECT: the per-device snapshot event — one `device.inventory` per device per pass, fattened at enqueue
